title: macOS 27.2 beta 1 now available to developers, here’s what’s new - 9to5Mac
author: Marcus Mendes
content:
![](https://9to5mac.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/09/macOS-27.2-b1.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=1600) 
Now that macOS 27 Golden Gate is officially out, Apple is moving on to its next beta cycle, straight to macOS 27.2 beta 1. Here are the details.
macOS 27.2 beta 1 now available
After releasing macOS 27 Golden Gate earlier this week, Apple is now rolling out the first developer beta of macOS 27.2, skipping over the 27.1 betas.
As for what to expect from this release, during its “Surprise and Shine” event earlier this month, Apple said that the new Siri AI, which launched in English, would expand to five more languages in October, including French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. This means developers might find these languages in this first beta.
Additionally, Apple has yet to confirm a new rollout date for two features it announced during WWDC but didn’t make it to the first macOS 27 release: an agentic feature in Passwords that will automatically change leaked passwords, and suggestions in Messages conversations.
We are digging through the code to check whether these made it to macOS 27.2 beta 1 and will report back with what we find.
macOS 27.2 beta 1 release build is 26B5086k.
Installing macOS 27.2 beta 1
![](https://9to5mac.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/09/macos27.2-b1.jpg?quality=82&strip=all)
Here’s how to install the first macOS 27.2 beta 1:
- Back up your Mac
- Open System Settings
- Go to General ⇾ Software Update
- Click the ‘i’ icon next to Beta Updates
- From the dropdown menu in the top-right, select the macOS Developer Golden Gate Beta
- Hit ‘Done’
Did you spot anything new in today’s macOS 27.2 Golden Gate beta 1? Let us know in the comments.
Worth checking out on Amazon
![Add 9to5Mac as a preferred source on Google](https://9to5mac.com/wp-content/themes/ninetofive/dist/images/google-preferred-source-badge-dark.png) 
![Add 9to5Mac as a preferred source on Google](https://9to5mac.com/wp-content/themes/ninetofive/dist/images/google-preferred-source-badge-light.png) 
FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More.
![](https://9to5mac.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/09/09-10-iPhone-18-Pro-Ghost-Banner.png)
summary: Apple has released the first developer beta of macOS 27.2, skipping the 27.1 beta cycle shortly after rolling out macOS 27 Golden Gate. The new beta build is 26B5086k and can be installed via System Settings under Software Update. Developers are currently investigating the code to see if it includes expanded Siri AI languages or previously delayed WWDC features.
key_points: Apple released macOS 27.2 beta 1 to developers with build number 26B5086k.
The release skips the macOS 27.1 beta cycle following the rollout of macOS 27 Golden Gate.
The update may include expanded Siri AI support for French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.
Developers are checking whether delayed WWDC features like automatic leaked password changes and Messages suggestions are present.

title: With iOS 27, Apple Is Laying the Groundwork to Paywall Your iPhone
author: Gabriel Zamora
content:
![](https://sm.pcmag.com/t/pcmag_uk/opinion/w/with-ios-2/with-ios-27-apple-is-laying-the-groundwork-to-paywall-your-i_us2z.1920.jpg) (Credit: Eric Zeman)
Historically, the annual iOS rollout acts as the great equalizer: Whether you're holding a brand-new flagship or a three-year-old device, updating your software feels like a free upgrade. But look closely at the iPhone over the last few years, and you'll see fault lines beginning to form.
Ever since Apple entered the relentless silicon arms race on phones, it has widened the gap between its standard processors and its ultra-premium chips. Newer hardware generations leave previous ones in the dust. We used to upgrade our phones for better cameras and speed. Lately, though, we're upgrading just to keep our software from feeling second-class.
With iOS 27, that slow burn has reached a boiling point. Apple’s latest operating system introduces a brutal new economic division. It splits iPhone owners into a three-tier caste system based on hardware age, RAM capacity, and eventually, the thickness of their wallets.
Siri AI Is Genius, Exclusionary Tech
I experienced this division firsthand. I downloaded the iOS 27 update, unlocked my phone, and immediately swiped through my Home Screen looking for the marquee feature. Where was the new standalone Siri AI app? Why did my device look exactly the same? As it turns out, I had to open my settings, scroll down, and manually register for a waitlist just to get in line for my phone's new brain.
Once I got past the gate, I put the new Siri AI to the test. I wanted to push its limits, so I initiated a complex brainstorming session about a steam-powered airship concept. To my genuine surprise, Siri was incredible: The fluid, natural back-and-forth resembled an advanced generative AI chatbot workspace. It is, without a doubt, a fantastic and genuinely useful tool to have built into a smartphone.
But a much larger, uglier truth quickly overshadowed my optimism: If you don't belong to the right iPhone caste, you are locked out. If you're on an iPhone 15 or older, you don't get this technology. My own iPhone 15 Pro barely made the cut, and by next year, I can't be sure it still will.
![](https://sm.pcmag.com/pcmag_uk/photo/s/siri-ai-in/siri-ai-in-action_1uwn.jpg) (Credit: Apple/PCMag)
Inside Apple's Uncomfortable iPhone Caste System
To understand the new three-tier iPhone ecosystem is to understand a structure of deliberate digital segregation. Apple has fractured its user base along lines of hardware age, spending power, and how quickly you adopt new tech. It's no longer about owning an iPhone; it's about which class of iPhone you can afford to stay in.
At the bottom of this new hierarchy are the grandfathered iPhones. Apple boasts that iOS 27 supports legacy devices all the way back to the iPhone 11. But if you own a standard iPhone 15 or older, you get optimizations, not new features. Look past the faster app launches, and you'll realize your phone isn’t getting smarter. You are locked out of the Siri AI workspace.
The middle tier would be any more recent iPhone, such as the 15 Pro, the base iPhone 16 or 17, and so on. But the fragmentation doesn't stop at artificial intelligence. iOS 27 introduces a variant of the OS that's strictly designed to reward the highest spenders. At the apex of this hierarchy, in the highest tier, is the newly unveiled iPhone Duo class.
For years, Apple power users have practically begged for basic productivity features, such as the ability to run two applications simultaneously. Apple repeatedly restricted the feature, treating split-screen multitasking as a sacred boundary reserved only for the iPad or a desktop.
But the adaptive version of iOS 27 on the iPhone Duo shatters that philosophy. Unfold the Duo’s massive canvas, and iOS 27 unlocks native, side-by-side app multitasking with unique app-pairing engines. By gating a baseline software feature like split-screen multitasking behind an eye-watering price tag, Apple is sending a clear message: Basic digital efficiency is no longer an inherent part of the smartphone experience. Instead, it’s an upmarket luxury.
Apple Intelligence Is a Trojan Horse
Even if you hold an iPhone with enough RAM to clear the AI gateway and join the middle tier, such as the brand-new iPhone 18 Pro Max, you're only safe for now. Though Apple doesn't consider your device obsolete just yet, the powerful AI features you enjoy with iOS 27 may well be subject to future restrictions. Tucked away in the official footnotes of Apple's launch documentation is a philosophical shift: Server-side features like Siri AI and Image Playground are subject to daily usage limits.
![](https://sm.pcmag.com/pcmag_uk/photo/t/the-new-si/the-new-siri-app-lets-you-revisit-past-conversations-or-star_e5wh.jpg) (Credit: Apple)
Apple is giving users a temporary, free taste of a truly intelligent assistant right now to hook them into the workflow. But the billing tollbooth is already being built. Apple's own terms explicitly state that "increased access to such features will be available for a fee" in the future.
By the time the next software cycle hits, Apple will flip the switch and demand a paid subscription for extended access to your phone’s own brain. If you want to keep using the excellent conversational assistant that just helped you map out a steampunk airship, you’ll have to pay a recurring fee or buy into the elite hardware tier.
Silicon Valley has spent years trying to turn physical hardware into a recurring software subscription. With iOS 27, Apple is finally doing it, and the iPhone may never be the same.
summary: Apple's iOS 27 creates a new three-tier ecosystem that divides iPhone users based on hardware age, RAM capacity, and spending power. Advanced features like the new Siri AI workspace and split-screen multitasking are restricted to newer, higher-end devices or locked behind exclusive hardware classes like the iPhone Duo. Additionally, Apple's documentation indicates that server-side AI features will eventually be subjected to daily usage limits and future paid subscriptions.
key_points: iOS 27 introduces a three-tier caste system that separates iPhone users based on hardware capabilities and spending power.
Owners of the iPhone 15 and older are largely locked out of the new standalone Siri AI workspace.
Split-screen multitasking is gated behind the expensive, newly unveiled iPhone Duo class.
Apple's launch documentation hints that server-side AI features will eventually require a fee or subscription for extended access.

title: iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max Review: Fastest phones ever, variable aperture camera soars
author: Mark Spoonauer
content:
Tom's Guide Verdict
The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max raise the bar for performance in a phone with the new A20 Pro chip. You also get a versatile new variable aperture camera that takes brighter images and gives you more creative control. The battery life from both devices is awesome, too, and you get the fastest charging yet from an iPhone. You have to pay $100 more for both Pro phones, and they’re heavier than their predecessors, but overall these are easily the best phones money can buy.
Pros
- +Fastest chip in a phone
- +Variable aperture camera
- +New Pro controls
- +Super long battery life
- +Smarter Siri AI
- +Faster charging
Cons
- -$100 price hike
- -Heavier designs
Why you can trust Tom's Guide
The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max don’t have a ‘wow’ feature to flex to your friends like the iPhone Duo. Yet beneath the familiar design is a pretty big leap forward for two areas people really care about: cameras and performance.
With a new variable aperture main camera, the iPhone 18 Pro lets in more light and gives you more creative freedom than ever before with new Pro controls. And the A20 Pro chip — the first 2nm chip in a phone — delivers record-breaking speed that surpasses all Android flagships. Based on our testing, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max battery life is stellar, too. And with the new Siri AI on board these Pro phones are much more capable personal assistants.
![iPhone 18 Pro Performance & Battery TESTED: The A20 Pro Is Ridiculous! - YouTube](https://img.youtube.com/vi/QJVNbFMd-zQ/maxresdefault.jpg) 
The bad news? The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are noticeably heavier than their predecessors, and the prices are $100 higher for both models. But if you’ve been putting off that upgrade for a while, you'll find that both of these Pros are the best phones you can buy.
iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max: Specs
| Row 0 - Cell 0 | iPhone 18 Pro | iPhone 18 Pro Max | 
| Price | From $1,199 | From $1,299 | 
| Main Display | 6.3-inch Super Retina XDR display (2,622 x 1,206) | 6.9-inch Super Retina XDR display (2,868 x 1,320) | 
| Processor | A20 Pro | A20 Pro | 
| Storage | 256GB, 512GB, 1TB, 2TB | 256GB, 512GB, 1TB, 2TB | 
| RAM | 12GB | 12GB | 
| Front Camera | 18MP Center Stage camera (f/1.9) | 18MP Center Stage camera (f/1.9) | 
| Rear Cameras | 48MP main with variable aperture (f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, f/4), 48MP ultrawide (f/2.2), 48MP telephoto w/4x optical zoom (f/2.8) | 48MP main with variable aperture (f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, f/4), 48MP ultrawide (f/2.2), 48MP telephoto w/4x optical zoom (f/2.8) | 
| Battery Life Video Playback | Up to 36 hours | Up to 45 hours | 
| Charging | 60W, 35W wireless | 60W, 35W wireless | 
| Size | 5.91 x 2.83 x 0.34 inches (150.0 x 71.9 x 8.75 mm) | 6.43 x 3.07 x 0.34 inches (163.4 x 78.0 x 8.75 mm) | 
| Weight | 7.44 ounces (211 grams) | 8.78 ounces (249 grams) | 
| IP Rating | IP68 | IP68 | 
| Colors | Black, Silver, Glacier, Burgundy | Black, Silver, Glacier, Burgundy | 
iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max Performance: Fastest phones ever
 ![Apple iPhone 18 Pro Max shown in hand](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/VEw4CiZWCodwwRopC8qNoK.jpg) 
The A20 Pro chip isn’t just the world’s first 2nm chip inside a smartphone; it’s the fastest one we’ve ever tested, blowing away the Android competition.
You get a new CPU with two super cores that are up to 20% faster and four efficiency cores, a 7-core GPU that’s up to 40 percent faster (up from 6 cores) and a new dual 16-core Neural Engine for better AI performance. Plus, there’s a wider memory interface that provides up to 50% more internal bandwidth.
It’s all wrapped up in a new package design that seats the memory next to the SoC instead of on top, which results in better heat dissipation. In fact, the vapor chamber itself has 3x the surface area to deliver better sustained performance (aka, less overheating). So how about the results? They’re pretty staggering.
| Row 0 - Cell 0 | Geekbench 6 (single/multi-core) | Geekbench 7 | 3DMark Solar Bay Unlimited | Geekbench AI 1.7 | 
| iPhone 18 Pro | 4,735 / 12,800 | 4,022 / 11,543 | 61.93 fps / 16,288 | 69245 (Quantitized Core ML/Neural Engine) | 
| iPhone 18 Pro Max | 4,741 / 12,789 | 4,025 / 11,525 | 67.9 fps/17,850 | 71974 | 
| Galaxy S26 Ultra | 3,785 / 11,563 | 3,149 / 10,612 | 49.37 fps / 12,984 | 83047 (TensorFlow Lite QNN) | 
| iPhone 17 Pro | 3,834/ 9,988 | 3,138 / 8,692 | 46.4 fps / 12,208 | 49,050 | 
| iPhone 17 Pro Max | 3,871 / 9,968 | 3,285 / 8,999 | 46.6 fps / 12,260 | 48549 | 
On Geekbench 6, which measures overall performance, the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max scored in the 4,700 range in the single core portion. That’s about 25% higher than the iPhone 17 Pro series and also 25% faster than the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy chip.
Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.
In terms of multi-core performance, the A20 Pro once again excelled, offering a 28% boost versus the iPhone 17 Pros. And we’re talking about a 10% advantage over the Galaxy S26 Ultra here.
We also ran the newer Geekbench 7, which has a multi-core benchmark that’s designed to be more real-world and uses more challenging data sets. The iPhone 18 Pro delivered similar performance gains.
The graphics leap is even more impressive from the A20 Pro. On the 3DMark Solar Bay Unlimited test, the iPhone 18 Pro turned in a frame rate of 62 fps, which is 33% faster than the 17 Pro. And the iPhone 18 Pro Max scored an even higher 67.9 fps, which is 45% faster than the 17 Pro Max.
The Galaxy S26 Ultra just couldn’t keep up, as the regular iPhone 18 Pro was 25% faster and the iPhone 18 Pro Max was 37% higher.
 ![Apple iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max shown in hand](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/36uFQPaegizL2WM4jr82pH.jpg) 
When playing the game Ungodly, the gameplay remained fluid even while I was slicing through three enemies at once with my sword. And the animations looked just as crisp as console gameplay when I switched characters and rained down fire attacks on my enemies.
So how about Apple’s sustained performance claims? Thanks to the larger vapor chamber and design of the A20 Pro chip, Apple promises up to a 40% improvement. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max did indeed impress when we ran the 3DMark Wild Life Extreme Stress Test, which loops through a graphics test 20 times in a row.
| Sustained Performance |  | 
|---|---|
| Row 0 - Cell 0 | 3DMark Wild Life Extreme Stress Test Stability Score | 
| iPhone 18 Pro | 62.8% | 
| iPhone 18 Pro Max | 79.4% | 
| Galaxy S26 Ultra | 53.9% | 
| iPhone 17 Pro | 61.1% | 
| iPhone 17 Pro Max | 65.2% | 
The iPhone 18 Pro Max turned in a stability score of 79.4%, which is 25% better than the iPhone 17 Pro Max. That’s also over 47% better than the Galaxy S26 Ultra. However, we saw only a minor 1.7% gain between the iPhone 17 Pro and 18 Pro.
Last but not least we tested AI performance using the Geekbench AI test. The iPhone 18 Pro turned in a Neural Engine score of 69,245 and the iPhone 18 Pro Max a much higher 71,974. That’s a boost of 41 to 48%, which means on-device AI tasks should run faster.
iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max: Battery life and charging
 ![Apple iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max shown in hand](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/sQDrYHT2bXbjRsmmPzXQaJ.jpg) 
Thanks to the efficiency of the A20 Pro chip and bigger batteries, the iPhone 18 Pro Max is rated to have the longest battery life ever of any iPhone. And the iPhone 18 Pro is rated for the endurance of last year’s iPhone 17 Pro Max, which made our best phone battery life list last year.
The good news is that both the iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone 18 Pro last longer than their 17 Pro counterparts. But we didn’t see a huge leap in endurance.
| Row 0 - Cell 0 | Hrs:Mins | 
| iPhone 18 Pro Max | 18:27 | 
| iPhone 18 Pro | 16:17 | 
| iPhone 17 Pro Max | 17:54 | 
| iPhone 17 Pro | 15:21 | 
| Galaxy S26 Ultra | 16:40 | 
| OnePlus 15 | 25:13 | 
On the Tom’s Guide battery test, which involves continuous web surfing over 5G on 150 nits of screen brightness, the iPhone 18 Pro Max lasted 18 hours and 41 minutes on its longest run and averaged 18:27. The iPhone 17 Pro Max lasted 17:54.
The iPhone 18 Pro lasted an average of 16:17 on our test, which is nearly an hour longer than the iPhone 17 Pro (15:21).
By comparison, the Galaxy S26 Ultra averaged 16:40 with the display mode set to standard and 16:10 in adaptive mode. So the iPhone 18 Pro Max lasts about 2 hours longer on a charge.
The OnePlus 15 is still the champ with its silicon carbon battery at 25 hours and 13 minutes. It will be interesting to see what happens when (or if) Apple embraces this technology for itself.
The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max both support 60W charging for the first time, and Apple promises a 30% charge in just 15 minutes. The iPhone 18 Pro hit 53% in 15 minutes and 80% in 30 minutes, but the iPhone 18 Pro Max was a bit behind with 44% and 77%, respectively.
iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max Cameras: What variable aperture can do
 ![Apple iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max shown in hand](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/b2pgpnQKaxpBNTMcJ7oQjK.jpg) 
The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max have a first for iPhones, even though the Samsung Galaxy S9 tried it years ago. I’m talking about a variable aperture main camera. There’s six tiny blades inside the wide lens that can expand or contract depending on the conditions.
For example, if you’re taking a portrait, the aperture might open up to f/1.48 to let in more light. And if you want more detail throughout the shot, the iPhone 18 Pro Max might stop down to f/4.0. This gives you more depth of field.
The iPhone 18 Pro’s camera can do this all automatically, but there’s new Pro controls on board that lets you set the exact aperture with four options.
![iPhone 18 Pro Max aperture f/4.0](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/SGfp5XiUJsGDo2kUU43cob-1200-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max aperture f/1.8](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/QVLjmGvb9JGFx8FxZ8ByVb-1200-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max aperture f/4.0](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/SGfp5XiUJsGDo2kUU43cob-1280-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max aperture f/1.8](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/QVLjmGvb9JGFx8FxZ8ByVb-1280-80.jpg) 
In the above portrait, you can see that the menu in the background is blurred out at f/1.48, but it's clear when I set it to f/4.
 ![photo of flowers in Bryant Park in front of stage](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/2CVrvHDZ35dFvy9xEo78rX.jpg) 
When I captured a photo of begonias in Bryant Park, I selected f/1.48 to blur the background and f/4.0 to bring detail to the stage across the park and buildings.
The wider aperture of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max also enables the phones to let in significantly more light overall, which means better low-light images.
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/XThNBx9PUHMu43tZ7KXvib-1200-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/NYycWYrSVQm4kL4CMRWqVb-1200-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/PS6QSXpornvyno7hLNKeCa-1200-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/XThNBx9PUHMu43tZ7KXvib-1280-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/NYycWYrSVQm4kL4CMRWqVb-1280-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/PS6QSXpornvyno7hLNKeCa-1280-80.jpg) 
Take this American flag photo captured in near darkness. You can make out more detail in the flag pole and the brick in the iPhone 18 Pro image. The Galaxy S26 Ultra shot is downright blurry.
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/9wpEQa3DwhwP4D3HH5A87b-1200-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/M7g2su3MgqDhzvuQbZbSVb-1200-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/9wpEQa3DwhwP4D3HH5A87b-1280-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/M7g2su3MgqDhzvuQbZbSVb-1280-80.jpg) 
Indoors I’d give a slight edge to the iPhone 18 Pro with this shot of Halloween decorations. The dots of light reflecting off the transparent orb look sharper through the iPhone. But the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s photo has more saturated colors inside the ball and in the fabric.
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/UaBpbCqvrKtnvGjwpz92Qc-1200-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/f5pR7L5C9dFRbT23GnhJLc-1200-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/eSTAqV88gqTcQTtsx2PHNc-1200-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/UaBpbCqvrKtnvGjwpz92Qc-1280-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/f5pR7L5C9dFRbT23GnhJLc-1280-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/eSTAqV88gqTcQTtsx2PHNc-1280-80.jpg) 
As you can see in the gallery above, the iPhone 18 Pro takes a better looking shot of produce (the red peppers don’t look right through the Samsung).
When it comes to zoom power, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max hold their own with a 4x telephoto lens and 8x optical quality zoom. The iPhone is neck and neck with Samsung with this 10x zoom shot of a pumpkin.
However, at 40x the iPhone really struggles versus the S26 Ultra. Check out the sign above. I'm sure the Galaxy is doing some AI processing, but the test is definitely sharper in its photo.
iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max: Video
My favorite video feature when testing the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max is the ability to add Cinematic mode to your clips after the fact. You no longer have to select the mode before you start shooting.
![iPhone 18 Pro: Cinematic Mode on - YouTube](https://img.youtube.com/vi/t7LuoywmKb0/maxresdefault.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro: Cinematic Mode off - YouTube](https://img.youtube.com/vi/-XgH2ozgkDU/maxresdefault.jpg) 
I had someone capture a video of me walking down a park trail. Afterwards, I toggled the Cinematic mode feature in editing right at the top of the screen. Sure enough, the iPhone 18 Pro added an artful blur to the footage.
Other new features include 4K Timelapse in Dolby Vision HDR, higher-quality low-light video in 1080p resolution and Pro controls for video, such as shutter speed.
![iPhone 18 Pro: Daylight (4K, 30 fps, HDR) - YouTube](https://img.youtube.com/vi/wGhxKbJTPPc/maxresdefault.jpg) 
To test out the iPhone 18 Pro’s video capabilities I shot this koi pond with a fountain using the new iPhone and Galaxy S26 Ultra at 4K at 30 fps with HDR turned on. I prefer the way the iPhone 18 Pro renders the details in the rocks and its smoother zooming motion; the S26 Ultra takes a second to regain focus. However, the S26 Ultra’s superior zoom shines when I get really close on the fountain wall.
![Galaxy S26 Ultra: Daylight (4K, 30 fps, HDR) - YouTube](https://img.youtube.com/vi/WbWvPo_lHrs/maxresdefault.jpg) 
iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max: Siri AI and Apple Intelligence
 ![Siri AI on an iPhone 18 Pro](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/UHFLgbZkizWAuzbea6ATRH.jpg) 
I’m not going to say that Siri AI is smarter than Gemini or ChatGPT yet, but it’s come a long way with iOS 27, and is now a lot more helpful. That’s because Siri now better understands your personal context, and it can let you do multiple things with a single voice prompt.
For example, I asked Siri to look up reviews for a hotel I was thinking of staying at with my brother for a road trip and send them via text in the same prompt. The results seemed okay but didn’t have as much detail as I’d like. So I tried again, asking for best dishes.
I can also control three different apps with the same prompt, such as setting a reminder, starting a timer and looking up photos and adding them to a Note. The new Siri AI is smarter and more powerful, but sometimes it started doing the first thing I asked before I got to the second request, interrupting the flow.
Visual Intelligence also gets an upgrade with iOS 27 and the iPhone 18 Pros. For example, I pointed the iPhone 18 Pro Max at a flyer with a bunch of dates on it, and it automatically recognized the dates and asked if I wanted to add them to my calendar. I especially like that there’s a dedicated Siri mode in the camera app so you don’t have to go to a separate app.
However, Siri AI is not quite as robust as Gemini or ChatGPT Voice. You can’t have a live back-and-forth conversation about what’s live in your camera view. This comes in quite handy for troubleshooting.
Other helpful Apple Intelligence features include contextually relevant cards that pop up when you’re texting. For example, you might get a prompt to add something to your calendar or reminders with a little icon.
Some of the coolest Apple Intelligence upgrades live in the camera app. For example, with Reframe you can change the angle of your photo after the fact. I did this with a photo of my daughter and the iPhone 18 Pro Max basically guessed what the background was of the pier and filled it in.
In addition, you can extend the background of your photos via Apple Intelligence. I tried this with a group shot of me, TechRadar’s Lance Ulanoff and Apple’s CEO John Ternus and Joz. It added a plant that wasn’t there and extended Lance’s arm. It’s a bit cool but also kinda creepy. Clean Up also gets a performance boost, making it faster to remove unwanted objects or people from your photos.
iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max: Design and colors
 ![Apple iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max shown in hand](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/4ALsrPjxc7ma3q24FGt74K.jpg) 
Most people would find it challenging to tell the difference between the iPhone 18 Pro series and iPhone 17 Pro phones. But there’s a couple of telltale signs.
First, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max have new colors, and Apple has done a better job of color matching the plateau and back glass of these phones. It’s no longer a two-tone look. I tested the Glacier (blue) version of the iPhone 18 Pro Max and the Burgundy iPhone 18 Pro. I prefer the Glacier, but Burgundy has a sophistication to it. You can also take your pick from Black or Silver.
 ![iPhone 18 Pro Max Dynamic Island](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/YFaQPPunbPf8e2qXHbeL55.jpg) 
The other key visual change is a smaller Dynamic Island. Apple moved the infrared sensor for Face ID under the display, allowing for a tinier cutout at the top of the display. Plus, you can now have up to three Live activities running at once inside the Dynamic Island area, such as a timer, Spotify and Uber status.
| Row 0 - Cell 0 | Weight | 
| iPhone 18 Pro | 7.44 oz (211 g) | 
| iPhone 18 Pro Max | 8.78 oz (249 g) | 
| iPhone 17 Pro | 7.27 oz (206 g) | 
| iPhone 17 Pro Max | 8.22 oz (233 g) | 
Perhaps owing to the bigger batteries, variable aperture lens camera and larger vapor chambers, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are heftier than their predecessors despite having the same dimensions as before. At least they fit in the same cases as the 17 Pro series if you're upgrading.
iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max: Displays
 ![Apple iPhone 18 Pro Max](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/dgQFoMHqkAGoahKiFKYdrd.jpg) 
The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max once again offer 6.3-inch and 6.9-inch displays with 120Hz refresh rates and rated 3,000 nits of maximum brightness. These panels are identical versus the iPhone 17 Pro series, but if you’re coming from an iPhone 16 Pro or Pro Max you’ll appreciate the anti-reflective coating.
In our lab tests, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max delivered strong results. Using our Klein K10-A probe combined with the Patterns Mobile iOS app, we measured a maximum brightness of 2,326 nits in a 25% window and 1,762 nits in a 10% window. The iPhone 18 Pro hit a similar 2,314 and 1,627.
 ![Apple iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone 17 Pro Max shown in hand](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/4edCqgzDe6Geozici7QFqK.jpg) 
The iPhone 17 Pro Max scored 2,324 in a 25% window and 1,882 at 10%, so comparable performance. We have not yet tested the iPhone 17 Pro for comparison.
The Galaxy S26 Ultra doesn’t support the Patterns Mobile app, but we measured HDR brightness in a 10% window with the same equipment. It reached 1,478 nits.
iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone Duo
 ![Apple iPhone Duo shown in hand](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/ENFN2u4hpSYiQYfbA6WbcL.jpg) 
If you’re on the fence between the $1,299 iPhone 18 Pro Max and $1,999 iPhone Duo, here’s a quick cheat sheet. The iPhone 18 Pro Max is the phone to get if you want a telephoto camera for better zooming and the longest possible battery life. Plus, only the iPhone 18 Pro Max offers Face ID; the Duo uses Touch ID.
The iPhone Duo is the phone for you if you want the ability to have a small phone and tablet in the same device. You get a larger 7.6-inch main display, versus 6.9 inches on the iPhone 18 Pro Max, plus the ability to run two apps side by side. It’s the better choice for watching videos and multitasking.
Verdict
 ![Apple iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max shown in hand](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/ZhVLRJCFGxVjGeDa3TaWmK.jpg) 
My take on the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max is that they are obscenely powerful phones inside a quiet redesign. You get the fastest chip ever in a phone with the A20 Pro, a variable aperture camera I find easy to use and overdue Pro controls that give you more creative freedom when shooting photos and videos.
I personally really like the ability to transform your pics and clips after the fact, whether it’s reframing your shots or adding a Cinematic effect to your footage. And while Siri AI is no Gemini killer, Apple has made great strides with its assistant to the point where it’s a lot more helpful in the moment. I can guarantee you’ll wind up using other chatbots less.
Between the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, I’d opt for the Pro Max because of the bigger screen and longer battery life, but the regular 18 Pro is no slouch and an hour better than the 17 Pro based on our testing.
I think the Galaxy S26 Ultra is still the phone to beat when it comes to zooming power and AI features, but it’s not nearly as fast as the iPhone 18 Pros and lasts two hours less on a charge versus the Max.
Sure, Apple is expected to completely reinvent the iPhone with the iPhone XX/iPhone 20 next year with a rumored all-screen design. But if you want the most powerful iPhone ever in a familiar body, the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are easily the best non-folding phones money can buy.
![Mark Spoonauer](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/wtAspSzVfcKLB4JEd39AMo.jpg) 
Mark Spoonauer is the global editor in chief of Tom's Guide and has covered technology for over 20 years. In addition to overseeing the direction of Tom's Guide, Mark specializes in covering all things mobile, having reviewed dozens of smartphones and other gadgets. He has spoken at key industry events and appears regularly on TV to discuss the latest trends, including Cheddar, Fox Business and other outlets. Mark was previously editor in chief of Laptop Mag, and his work has appeared in Wired, Popular Science and Inc. Follow him on Twitter at @mspoonauer.

summary: The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max introduce major performance and camera upgrades driven by the new A20 Pro chip and a versatile variable aperture main camera. Both devices deliver impressive battery life, faster charging support up to 60W, and improved AI performance. However, the new models come with a $100 price increase and heavier physical designs compared to their predecessors.
key_points: Powered by the A20 Pro chip, the iPhone 18 Pro models offer record-breaking processing speeds and superior graphics performance.
The new variable aperture main camera allows for better low-light photography and enhanced creative control over depth of field.
Both Pro models feature longer battery life and support 60W fast charging for the first time.
The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are $100 more expensive and noticeably heavier than previous generations.

title: The iPhone 18 Pro’s big camera update is all about the small gains
author: Allison Johnson
content: Last week, Apple announced an iPhone unlike any it has made in the past. An iPhone that has seemingly already led several other phone manufacturers to pursue entirely different designs for their flagship products. A remarkably distinct device with the kind of “I can’t believe they did that” software touches that Apple sometimes pulls off when it’s at the top of its game. The iPhone 18 Pro’s big camera update is all about the small gains The Pro camera’s major upgrade offers minor image quality improvements — whether or not you know what an f-stop is. That phone is not the iPhone 18 Pro. The 18 Pro and Pro Max are in the unusual position of being the second-most interesting iPhones that Apple is launching this year. The foldable iPhone Duo stole the show at Apple’s launch event, but it’s not arriving until next month. In the meantime, the 18 Pro cometh, and it is extremely familiar even with a totally new hardware feature in the camera. It is so similar to the iPhone 17 Pro that it can use the same cases. Have you used an iPhone 17 Pro? Great, you now know what it’s like to use the 18 Pro. There are no surprises, and unless you’re a truly committed smartphone photographer, no hugely compelling reason to pick an 18 Pro over a 17 Pro if you can find one on sale. It’s what we’ve come to expect from what was the flagship iPhone: excellent and utterly iterative. ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268735_iPhone_18_Pro_AKrales_0542.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=16.666666666667%2C0%2C66.666666666667%2C100&w=2400) ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268735_iPhone_18_Pro_AKrales_0542.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400) 8 Verge Score The Good - Manual exposure controls in the native camera app, finally - Marginal improvements to image quality - Photographing sunstars with a smartphone camera rules The Bad - $100 more expensive than last year - Manual exposure controls are tiny - Higher storage tiers are quite pricey ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268735_iPhone_18_Pro_MAX_AKrales_1087.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=16.666666666667%2C0%2C66.666666666667%2C100&w=2400) ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268735_iPhone_18_Pro_MAX_AKrales_1087.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400) 8 Verge Score The Good - Manual exposure controls in the native camera app, finally - Marginal improvements to image quality - Photographing sunstars with a smartphone camera rules The Bad - $100 more expensive than last year - Manual exposure controls are tiny - Higher storage tiers are quite pricey Inside, the iPhone 18 Pro has a revamped thermal management design that allows its new A20 Pro chip to sustain full performance for longer, but the biggest truly new idea is inside the main camera, where Apple has added a moving aperture to control how much light hits the sensor. This is a big deal, and also a small deal, which I promise makes sense. With a few exceptions, phone cameras have fixed apertures. Their sensors and lenses are so small that most of your scene is in focus even when you’re shooting wide open, and it’s usually best to get as much light as you can on that tiny sensor anyway. But there are some edge cases where a narrower aperture is helpful, even on a phone camera. It could also be helpful in other situations, particularly in low light, to open up the aperture even further than the iPhone’s traditional f/1.8. So Apple seems to have said, “Screw it. Let’s have it both ways,” and put in a variable aperture. ![With the right lighting and the help of a macro lens you can see those aperture blades.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268735_iPhone_18_Pro_AKrales_0637.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400) So there are really two separate things happening here. The maximum aperture is now bigger, at f/1.48 vs. f/1.8, and has the ability to get smaller, with stops available at f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4. And while both the larger and smaller apertures do offer marginal improvements to photo quality in some cases, the differences are generally marginal. One of the reasons photographers like a wider aperture is for its ability to throw more of the background of a photo out of focus. But the small lens and sensor on a smartphone camera don’t allow for the same kind of soft background blur you get from a bigger camera system. At the iPhone’s old maximum aperture of f/1.8, most things are in focus most of the time, and going to the slightly wider f/1.48 doesn’t make a huge difference. ![iPhone 18 Pro, f/1.48 cropped to 100 percent](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_1835_100.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![iPhone 18 Pro, f/1.8 cropped to 100 percent](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_1837_100.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) A bigger aperture does offer an advantage for low light photography. On a traditional camera, letting in more light allows the system to keep noise down by using a faster shutter speed, a lower ISO, or both. It’s not quite the same on a smartphone camera that’s combining multiple frames at different exposures to create the final image, but broadly the concept of “more light = better photo” holds. Maybe because phones are already so good at coping with low light through these computational methods, the low light gains in the 18 Pro look pretty minor. If I look closely at the detail in a shot at f/1.48 versus f/1.8, I can see a difference, but it’s subtle. ![iPhone 18 Pro at f/1.8, cropped to 100 percent](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_2323_100.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![iPhone 18 Pro at f/1.48, cropped to 100 percent](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_2322_100.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) The biggest advantage might be for Night Mode. At f/1.48, the system can use a slightly shorter Night Mode capture time compared to f/1.8. That’s less time you have to try and keep your hand still and less noise that the system needs to try and process out. ![iPhone 18 Pro, f/1.48 and 1.4 second night mode capture, cropped to 100 percent](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_2353_f1p5_100.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![iPhone 18 Pro, f/1.8 and 2.2 second night mode capture, cropped to 100 percent](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_2354_f1p8_100.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) On the other side of the dial, a smaller aperture is useful for extending depth of field and keeping more stuff in focus, particularly if your subject is close to the camera. If you’re taking a close-up photo of a statue, at f/1.48 or f/1.8 the back part of it might look a bit soft. Stopping down to f/4 sharpens up the part in the background. ![iPhone 18 Pro at f/1.48. For a subject close to the lens, the background blur is more pronounced.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_1819.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![iPhone 18 Pro at f/4](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_1818.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![iPhone 18 Pro at f/1.48. For subjects farther from the camera, the wider aperture doesn’t have much of a softening effect to the background.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_1395.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![iPhone 18 Pro at f/4](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_1392.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) That’s helpful! But once again, you’ll find these benefits on the margins. That’s because the iPhone’s new f/1.48 maximum aperture actually equates to about f/5 on full frame in terms of depth of field, which already puts a lot of the stuff in front of and behind your subject in focus. Unless you’re really close to your subject, most things are in focus or close enough when you photograph them with a smartphone camera. If you don’t know or care about f-stops, you’ll still get along just fine with this updated camera. By default the aperture is set to automatically adjust based on lighting conditions, and it seems to stay at f/1.8 most of the time in good lighting. The aperture does open up to f/1.48 in dim light automatically, and will close down to f/4 when taking a group photo with someone who’s standing further back. And I saw it consistently dropping down to f/4 when I was taking a photo of some close-up text. That’s a situation where f/4 will help you get more in focus and make for a potentially more usable photo. But that’s an awfully narrow set of use cases, whether you’re the kind of person who wants to take manual control over the aperture or not. ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268735_iPhone_18_Pro_AKrales_0651.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400) ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268735_iPhone_18_Pro_AKrales_0659.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400) That’s the big update, and the effect is a relatively small one. But it’s not the only camera update. Friends, in the year of our Lord 2026, you can finally change the exposure controls by yourself in the iPhone camera app. Apple has added pro controls for the aforementioned aperture as well as shutter speed, white balance, and focus. There’s also the exposure compensation control that existed before, though no direct ISO adjustment, which someone coming from a traditional camera system would probably look for. But there’s enough control here for anyone who is so inclined to get a little more creative and hands-on with the stock app than ever before. I noticed that when I was using a manual shutter speed, the results appeared to have been less processed. Apple spokesperson Stephanie Ng confirmed that the camera is indeed capturing a single frame rather than using the typical multi-frame processing. That means you lose a bit of dynamic range, though the final image will still include a gain map if there are highlights bright enough to warrant it. That’s not ideal if you’re trying to capture detail in both highlights and shadows, but on the other hand, this is one way to get the less-processed iPhone photo that some folks have been clamoring for. It’s a bit hidden, but it’s finally here. ![A photo taken with automatic exposure settings.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_2235-vert.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![Taken with a manually selected shutter speed, which disables multi-frame HDR.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_2236-vert.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) On top of that, there’s a new set of texture controls for Photographic Styles, with the ability to add a film-inspired glow to highlight areas of your photo, overlay film grain, or soften skin. It’s another first for Apple: the ability to make your photos a little bit worse. But you know, tastefully, Film simulation modes for digital cameras are as popular as ever, and Apple is trying to catch that wave. The recently released Pixel 11 series includes so many ways to customize the look of your photos that their camera team had an escalation meeting about it. Likewise, Samsung has added any number of ways you can restyle your photo into what you envisioned it would be. After basically a decade of pushing the technological envelope year after year, the major phone manufacturers seem to be opening up to other definitions of image quality. If you put all these updates together alongside the less-important but completely underrated addition of a first-party wrist strap (!) accessory for Apple’s own 18 Pro cases, maybe there’s something more camera than phone here. When I got my hands on the 18 Pro last week, I wondered if I could convince myself that the iPhone is a camera camera now. ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_1705.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_1786.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_1416.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_1406.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_1387.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_1477.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_1557.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_1593.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_1535.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_1549.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_1536.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_1544.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_1610.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_1756.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_1580.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_1620.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_1762.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_1654.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_1662.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) I will go so far as to say that I had a better time shooting with the 18 Pro than I’ve ever had using an iPhone camera in the past. I shot sunstars peeking out behind some leaves in Battery Park. I took it to the US Open and documented the excitement of a night match at Arthur Ashe Stadium. I took a video of a sizzling fajita plate and converted it to a cinematic masterpiece* after capture. But I never forgot I was using a phone. The pro control icons are pretty small on the 18 Pro’s screen, and I had to focus just to hit them properly. I had to dismiss a spam call in the middle of a shoot. And after a morning of battery-draining photo and video shooting, it became really important to top the battery off so as not to lose my lifeline to the rest of the world. It’s a step closer, and the moving aperture is a bit closer to that dream of a phone that’s also a camera. But it’s still a phone. *I use the term masterpiece loosely. ![wrist strap](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268735_iPhone_18_Pro_AKrales_0151.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400) Apple, Google, and Samsung have each achieved their own kind of excellence in shaping what a smartphone camera can be. So it’s interesting watching them pivot to flexibility and embracing some of the flaws that are turning people on to old digital cameras. But taking photos with one of their flagship phones still feels like using a phone, whether there are moving aperture blades inside or not. One of the reasons I found the wrist strap so appealing was that it made the process of handling the phone as a camera feel more like, well, a camera. I’m hoping for the day when one of the few phone makers who sell devices in the US at scale tries something like the Xiaomi photography kits or Vivo’s telephoto lenses. That would feel like a whole new camera experience. Apple is also using the 18 Pro to introduce something it calls Reference Image, which is a method the company has developed for verifying the authenticity of a photo taken on the iPhone. Apple will start using Google’s SynthID standard to tag photos with AI edits, but Reference Image comes at the problem from the other direction: helping people to identify which photos are real. Apple designed a new main camera sensor for the 18 Pro and Pro Max that adds encrypted data to the images it produces, so it’s limited to photos taken with the main camera on those two models. It’s complicated and clunky right now, but it also seems to be a pretty robust system with a lot of room to grow. ![In order to use the Reference Image feature, you need to turn it on in settings.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_2367.png?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![Where a Reference Image is attached to a file, this icon will appear near the top of the screen in the photos app.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_2369.png?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) You need to enable it as a camera mode in the settings app in order to use it, and then actively switch the camera app to Reference mode to capture a Reference Image. The resulting image file contains the encrypted data from the main sensor, which means it’s bigger than a normal photo — a standard 4MB image I shot of a city street is an 8MB file when I shoot it in reference mode. If you send a Reference Image to someone who wants to verify that a Reference Image hasn’t been tampered with, they can push a button to send it to Apple’s Private Cloud Compute, where that encrypted data will be “developed” showing the image basically as it came off the sensor. (Apple’s metaphor here is having the original negative of a traditional film photograph.) It’s hard to use at the moment, but the idea is that it’s almost impossible to tamper with. Apple is releasing an API for third-party developers to add an option to view reference photos when they’re attached to an image, and the company seems eager to push this into the wider ecosystem now that all of this has been announced. ![The 18 Pro’s glacier color grew on me but nothing beats burgundy.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268735_iPhone_18_Pro_MAX_AKrales_0839.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400) There are some meaningful updates on the video side of the aisle, too. There’s updated focus tracking that uses AI to stick to a subject. It’ll even pick them up if they leave the frame briefly and come back, but in my brief testing it seems to forget about someone if they’re gone for more than a few seconds. You can also convert video footage from the main camera to Cinematic after the fact, in the same way that you can convert regular photos to portrait mode after you take them. I often wish I’d taken video in cinematic mode but I never remember to in the moment, so this is a nice update. Video files don’t appear to be vastly bigger compared to similar clips from the 17 Pro, so this doesn’t come at a big cost to your storage space, either. And that’s no small thing. The 18 Pro and Pro Max are each $100 more this year, with the 18 Pro starting at $1,199 with 256GB of storage. But each jump in storage tier will cost you dearly — all the way up to a $2,399 version for 2TB. Likewise, the Pro Max starts at $1,299.99 with 256GB of storage and goes all the way up to $2,499 for the 2TB version. ![On the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the Dynamic Island shrinks down when not in use.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268735_iPhone_18_Pro_MAX_AKrales_0916.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400) You’re not getting nothing for that price hike. There’s a new chipset, the A20 Pro, plus an updated vapor chamber that’s supposed to move heat away from the chipset more effectively to help with sustained performance compared to the 17 Pro. I noted the phone getting pretty warm on my first few days of using it, which are usually pretty taxing as you’re going through setup, app downloads, and data indexing, but haven’t noticed it as a consistent problem. Battery life is the eternally impossible question to answer about a phone after a week of using it. I haven’t experienced anything like a “normal day” for the past week, but I haven’t seen any surprising battery drain from the 18 Pro in my downtime, either. It survived a day of intense use during a video shoot without a recharge at any point, which is no small feat. Apple quotes a modest gain in battery life for the smaller Pro model — 36 hours of video playback, up from 33 hours on the 17 Pro. The 18 Pro Max offers a bigger increase: 45 hours of video playback compared to 39 on the 17 Pro Max. Verge editor-in-chief Nilay Patel has been testing the Pro Max, and he says it’s been lasting more than a day, although he also noted the same early setup vibes. He also points out his 17 Pro Max battery was a champ when it was new and now can’t make it through a day after a year of heavy use, so the real test here is going to come much later in this phone’s life cycle. The real test here is going to come much later in this phone’s life cycle The 18 Pro I’m testing uses Apple’s new in-house C2 modem, marking the first time that a Pro iPhone has shipped with an Apple-made cellular chip. It seems that the homegrown stuff has finally cleared Apple’s quality bar for inclusion at the very high end, and I can’t say I’ve found any reason to fault it over the past week. The C2 is paired with the N1 wireless networking chip, and the system overall seems quick to jump off a Wi-Fi signal when I’m in an elevator and just as eager to pick up a cell signal when I step out. Here’s hoping it’s just as quick to ditch my home Wi-Fi when I’m in the carport outside of my house trying to start GPS navigation — truly, the dream. One other notable update here is that the Dynamic Island is smaller. On the 17 Pro, the black bar encompassed the Face ID sensor in addition to the front-facing camera. On the 18 Pro, the Face ID sensor is hidden under the regular part of the screen until that real estate is needed by the Dynamic Island. Apple went to great lengths to disguise the sensor under a unique pixel pattern that uses black pixels to allow the IR signals necessary for Face ID to pass through. Pretty cool, though I can’t say I noticed the Dynamic Island’s smaller size even a single time as I was using the phone, and jumping back to the 17 Pro’s larger Dynamic Island hasn’t bothered me. And I have yet to need three items in the Dynamic Island at one time, rather than two, but this is a new capability that exists on the 18 Pro. Possibly an even bigger deal than the launch of a new $1,200 phone is the release of iOS 27, and with it the new-new AI Siri. We previewed it in detail earlier this summer, and it continues to impress me. Particularly, its ability to search across email and messages all at once — this keeps feeling more and more like a superpower the longer I use it. We also noted when it debuted that Siri as an AI chatbot is much less chatty and eager to keep you engaged than the likes of Gemini or ChatGPT, which is something I also appreciate the more I use it. iOS 27 has just gone fully public this week, and it will be interesting to see how people take to the new Siri. It has a lot of work to do to earn the trust of the public that it can do anything more complex than setting a timer reliably, but Siri seems to be on the right track at least. Finally. ![The iPhone camera is more like a camera than ever before.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268735_iPhone_18_Pro_AKrales_0730.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400) Unlike Siri, the 18 Pro’s big hardware update is much less visible. The aperture is hard to see without the right light and the help of a macro lens. It’s as small as my thumbnail, and it’s under layers of optical glass. Most people who buy this phone probably won’t go looking for it, and that’s fine. It’s the kind of feature that can live in the background and just jump in to help here and there, unseen, when you need it. You don’t need to know what it is or how it works. Which is kind of the point of personal technology, anyway. So why make a big deal out of such a small thing? Is the defining feature of Apple’s new phones really an iris as thin as a human hair that most people will never see? I think two things are true at once: Adding a major new hardware feature to the world’s most popular camera is notable to those of us who pay attention to such things. But it’s also beside the point. ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268735_iPhone_18_Pro_AKrales_0083.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400) ![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268735_iPhone_18_Pro_AKrales_0333.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400) The iPhone camera’s most important job is to always take a usable photo, by default, no matter what. This new aperture mechanism provides some benefits to that end, and on top of that, allows a more hands-on photographer access to camera controls that weren’t there before. But the first part of that mission is the most important, and the 18 Pro upholds that mandate. Most people who use this phone will never touch the aperture control, and that’s fine. They might get a picture of a menu that’s fully in focus thanks to the camera dropping down to f/4, or a night shot that’s a little more detailed thanks to a brighter maximum aperture. Otherwise, it will feel like the same camera they’ve come to expect from a Pro iPhone. As long as you don’t expect a revolutionary new camera experience, then the 18 Pro is what it should be: a little better than the version that came before it.
summary: The iPhone 18 Pro features a familiar design and iterative updates, highlighted by a new variable aperture camera system. While the hardware allows for a wider f/1.48 maximum aperture and smaller stops down to f/4, the resulting image quality and depth-of-field improvements are largely subtle. Additionally, the native camera app now includes manual exposure controls and new photographic style textures.
key_points: The iPhone 18 Pro is physically very similar to the previous generation and retains case compatibility with the iPhone 17 Pro.
The main camera introduces a moving aperture system that ranges from f/1.48 to f/4 for variable light control.
Image quality and low-light improvements from the variable aperture are mostly marginal in everyday use.
The native camera app finally offers manual pro controls for aperture, shutter speed, white balance, and focus.
Using manual shutter speed disables multi-frame HDR processing, resulting in less processed photos.

title: iPhone 18 Pro Max vs iPhone 14 Pro Max: All the differences and should you upgrade?
author: John Velasco
content:
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs 14 Pro Max.](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/zQniEFCJPwZTgNapSzUwAB.jpg) 
People are holding onto their phones much longer than ever before, which isn't surprising given how prices keep rising. That’s at the heart of this iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 14 Pro Max comparison, as it raises the question of whether you should upgrade to the latest flagship.
I’ve said countless times that three years should be the bare minimum to wait before upgrading your phone. If you’re still rocking the iPhone 14 Pro Max, there’s more than enough incentive to make the jump to the iPhone 18 Pro Max — especially with a four-year gap between them.
iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 14 Pro Max: Specifications
| Header Cell - Column 0 | iPhone 18 Pro Max | iPhone 14 Pro Max | 
|---|---|---|
| Price | $1,299 | $1,099 | 
| Main Display | 6.9-inch Super Retina XDR display (2,868 x 1,320) | 6.7-inch Super Retina XDR display (2,796 x 1,290) | 
| Processor | A20 Pro | A16 Bionic | 
| Storage | 256GB, 512GB, 1TB, 2TB | 128GB, 256GB, 512GB, 1TB | 
| RAM | 12GB | Row 4 - Cell 2 | 
| Front Cameras | 18MP Center Stage camera (f/1.9) | 12MP (f/1.9) | 
| Rear Cameras | 48MP main with variable aperture (f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, f/4), 48MP ultrawide (f/2.2), 48MP telephoto w/4x optical zoom (f/2.8) | 48MP main (f/1.78), 12MP ultrawide (f/2.2), 12MP telephoto with 3x optical zoom (f/2.8) | 
| Battery Life Video Playback | Up to 45 hours | Up to 29 hours | 
| Size | 6.43 x 3.07 x 0.34 inches (163.4 x 78.0 x 8.75 mm) | 6.33 x 3.05 x 0.31 inches (160.7 x 77.6 x 7.85 mm) | 
| Weight | 8.78 ounces (249 grams) | 8.47 ounces (240 grams) | 
| IP Rating | IP68 | IP68 | 
| Colors | Black, Silver, Glacier, Burgundy | Space Black, Silver, Gold, Deep Purple | 
iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 14 Pro Max: Price and release
 ![iPhone 18 Pro Max](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/TUHKFKjf3sxjBNZKbzJu8o.jpg) 
When the iPhone 14 Pro Max launched on September 16, 2022, it started at $1,099 — whereas the iPhone 18 Pro Max sets you back $1,199. While this is much higher, you get 256GB of baseline storage with the newer model instead of the 128GB on the iPhone 14 Pro Max.
This comes out to about a 9.1% increase in starting price, which isn’t bad considering the four-year gap between the two. Preorders are open now for the iPhone 18 Pro Max, with official retail availability set for September 18.
iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 14 Pro Max: Design
 ![iPhone 14 Pro Max](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/q5UfaGNrEwWgTWH2iUdKMU.jpg) 
Put them side by side, and it’s obvious they share the same fundamental design language Apple has leaned on since the iPhone 12 Pro. Look closer, though, and key differences quickly surface.
For starters, the iPhone 14 Pro Max is notably thinner and lighter — a clear contrast to the denser, heftier feel of the new flagship. When you flip them over, the distinction is even more pronounced: the iPhone 18 Pro Max swaps the traditional corner module for an elongated camera island that stretches nearly the full width of the upper rear glass.
 ![iPhone 18 Pro Max](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/PsAoKzRkrmCg46aQ53ywDo.jpg) 
While it’s an evolutionary visual shift, several hardware refinements complete the package. Beyond a narrower Dynamic Island and trimmed-down display bezels, the newer phone adds the dedicated Camera Control key and the customizable Action Button. Together, these tweaks make the iPhone 18 Pro Max feel far more packed and purposeful.
Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.
iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 14 Pro Max: Display
 ![iPhone 14 Pro Max](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/s2wmNYVCKkamFwJV8mJdeT.jpg) 
The screen is another area where you clearly get more for your money. While the iPhone 14 Pro Max features a 6.7-inch Super Retina XDR display, the iPhone 18 Pro Max steps up to a larger 6.9-inch panel — giving you more visual real estate for gaming and streaming video on the go.
 ![iPhone 18 Pro Max](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/Yjffyuo5ef8MQZ2Juy52Co.jpg) 
Both panels support 120Hz ProMotion refresh rates for fluid UI animations, but visibility gets a massive boost on the newer flagship. The iPhone 14 Pro Max’s 2,000-nit peak brightness was no slouch, yet the 18 Pro Max pushes outdoor brightness to an even higher 3,000 nits.
Combined with an upgraded anti-reflective coating to combat direct glare and a more compact Dynamic Island that eats up less screen space, the newer display makes direct-sunlight viewing vastly superior.
iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 14 Pro Max: Cameras
 ![iPhone 14 Pro Max](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/Nr6f9HPS4ymafxtXRRSsfU.jpg) 
Out of everything, the camera system alone warrants making the leap from the 14 Pro Max to the 18 Pro Max. While the iPhone 14 Pro Max was the first in Apple’s stable to introduce a 48MP main sensor, the iPhone 18 Pro Max delivers substantial generational gains across its entire triple-lens array.
Leading the charge is the new variable physical aperture on the 48MP main camera. It lets shooters choose between four distinct aperture settings to dial in specific optical effects — from creamy, natural background bokeh to deep depth-of-field that keeps the entire frame in sharp focus.
 ![iPhone 18 Pro cameras](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/HYuuDMJ2Ch2YMUKD2MbYWc.jpg) 
Telephoto reach is another huge incentive. The iPhone 18 Pro Max upgrades to a sharper 48MP telephoto sensor with 4x optical zoom (up from the 14 Pro Max’s 12MP 3x shooter). Thanks to this folded-periscope setup, the new flagship stretches reach dramatically further to pull in vastly crisp detail on distant subjects.
Finally, serious shooters will appreciate the newly integrated Pro Controls, which put direct manual adjustments for shutter speed, white balance, ISO, and manual focus right at your fingertips. Throw in creator-grade video upgrades like 4K recording at 120 fps, ProRes capture, and Log profile support for color grading, and the iPhone 18 Pro Max easily establishes itself as a legitimate production camera I wouldn't mind keeping in my pocket.
iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 14 Pro Max: Performance
 ![iPhone 18 Pro Max](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/cTmx5d63stEFmgKNszEyDo.jpg) 
If you’re still rocking the iPhone 14 Pro Max, you’re running Apple’s A16 Bionic chipset. When we put it to the test back in 2022, it set the pace with a Geekbench multicore score of 5,333 and a 3DMark Wild Life Unlimited frame rate of 74 fps. While it was a clear class-leader at launch, the iPhone 18 Pro Max widens the gap dramatically with its next-generation, 2nm A20 Pro chip.
Although we still need to run the new phone through our rigorous lab testing, our expectations are set sky-high based on where Apple left off. Last year’s iPhone 17 Pro Max and its A19 Pro silicon delivered a Geekbench multicore score of 9,968 — a staggering 86.9% improvement over the 14 Pro Max.
That should widen even further with the iPhone 18 Pro Max, especially since the new processor is built on TSMC's cutting-edge 2-nanometer fabrication process.
iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 14 Pro Max: Battery and charging
 ![iPhone 18 Pro Max](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/6N7PRoZ922V5VYKySqDu7o.jpg) 
Endurance is another area where we'll likely see substantial gains with the iPhone 18 Pro Max. Four years is a massive gap in smartphone tech, and during that time, we’ve seen Apple make each successive iteration noticeably more power-efficient than the last.
When we put the iPhone 14 Pro Max through our custom battery test, it posted an impressive time of 13 hours and 39 minutes. Back in 2022, that runtime made it an easy contender for our best phone battery life list. However, the iPhone 18 Pro Max could set a new benchmark for longevity.
Last year’s iPhone 17 Pro Max lasted an astounding 17 hours and 54 minutes on the exact same test. That’s more than four hours longer. When you factor in the ultra-efficient, 2nm A20 Pro chip powering the iPhone 18 Pro Max, I wouldn't be surprised to see it comfortably cross the 18-hour threshold.
Charging gets a long-overdue overhaul, too. The iPhone 14 Pro Max was held back by Apple’s aging Lightning connector and sluggish 20W wired speeds, which only filled the cell to 42% after 30 minutes. The iPhone 18 Pro Max not only brings the universal versatility of USB-C, but it also ramps wired charging speeds up to 60W — which Apple claims can replenish 50% of the battery in just 15 minutes.
iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 14 Pro Max: Software and AI
 ![iPhone 18 Pro Max](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/PetgCsR77oez9YPGe9HZFo.jpg) 
Both devices run Apple’s new iOS 27 update, giving iPhone 14 Pro Max owners access to core interface refinements, refreshed home screen customizations, and system-level performance optimizations. But beneath that shared experience, the iPhone 18 Pro Max benefits from the platform's most transformative additions: Apple Intelligence and Siri AI.
Because Apple Intelligence requires substantial on-device processing muscle, the iPhone 14 Pro Max doesn’t make the cut — a massive trade-off given the sheer utility of this new suite. Adding to the divide is the revamped Siri AI, which proved far more conversational in my own testing with its multi-step task automation and onscreen awareness. Those capabilities make the assistant feel less like a rigid voice utility and more like an intuitive assistant I can actually rely on.
iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 14 Pro Max: Outlook
 ![iPhone 18 Pro Max](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/XEnBSEb3MMRqFRw7NPesBo.jpg) 
We still need to put the iPhone 18 Pro Max through our complete battery of tests to see if it’s indeed a top best phone contender, but everything we’ve seen so far points to an easy upgrade recommendation. Between the larger 6.9-inch display, game-changing variable-aperture camera, 60W USB-C charging, and exclusive access to Siri AI and Apple Intelligence, there’s a substantial collection of improvements that make jumping to the new flagship worthwhile.
Financially, that four-year upgrade cycle also makes plenty of practical sense. Exactly 48 months have passed since the iPhone 14 Pro Max hit shelves, meaning if you’ve managed to tuck away about $27.06 per month, you already have enough saved to cover the iPhone 18 Pro Max outright.
