summary: Apple's first foldable device, the iPhone Duo, has entered the market as a polished competitor to Android foldables, though it does not reinvent the form factor. While it features a matte display that effectively minimizes the crease and a competitively priced build, its hardware and software rely largely on existing concepts. The author expresses concern that Android manufacturers might rush to copy controversial design choices, such as the sidebar UI, but ultimately views Apple's entry as a net-positive that will drive industry creativity and accessory support.
key_points: Apple's iPhone Duo is a polished foldable device that enters the market as a strong competitor to Android foldables without fundamentally reinventing the form factor.
Hardware features include a matte display that nearly eliminates the visible crease, though it retains an under-display camera with a noticeable glossy dot.
Software highlights feature intuitive split-screen capabilities and a new sidebar UI that relocates app controls and the status bar, though this layout draws mixed reactions.
The author worries that Android manufacturers might hastily copy Apple's design choices, such as the potentially awkward sidebar setup.

Despite lacking groundbreaking innovations, the iPhone Duo is competitively priced and expected to positively impact the foldable market by pushing accessory makers and developers to take the form factor seriously.

title: iPhone Duo vs. iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone 18 Pro Max — here’s the one I recommend
author: John Velasco
content:
![iPhone Duo vs. iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone 18 Pro Max.](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/DRnLLVmpQuzzengDjXNSQb.jpg) 
Every year when Apple unveils its flagship lineup, people always ask me which one is worth their money. This year’s reveal at the "Surprise and Shine" event is no exception because Apple has completely upended the playbook by introducing its first-ever foldable, the iPhone Duo.
While refining the hardware and software is no doubt a huge undertaking on Apple’s part, the company still needs to convince buyers that it’s worth the premium over its two other flagships: the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. Deciding which flagship belongs in your pocket is a substantially tougher call, but I’m going to break down their specs, features, prices, and more to tell you which one truly deserves your money.
![I Tried the iPhone Duo... Is It Worth It? - YouTube](https://img.youtube.com/vi/2qNfOa5AuVU/maxresdefault.jpg) 
iPhone Duo vs. iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone 18 Pro Max: Specifications
| Header Cell - Column 0 | iPhone Duo | iPhone 18 Pro | iPhone 18 Pro Max | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Price | $1,999 | $1,199 | $1,299 | 
| Main Display | 7.6-inch Super Retina XDR (1,878 x 2,670) | 6.3-inch Super Retina XDR display (2,622 x 1,206) | 6.9-inch Super Retina XDR display (2,868 x 1,320) | 
| Outer Display | 5.4-inch Super Retina XDR (1,398 x 2,034) | N/A | N/A | 
| Processor | A20 Pro | A20 Pro | A20 Pro | 
| Storage | 256GB, 512GB, 1TB, 2TB | 256GB, 512GB, 1TB, 2TB | 256GB, 512GB, 1TB, 2TB | 
| RAM | 12GB | 12GB | 12GB | 
| Front Cameras | 12MP Center Stage outer (ƒ/2.2), 1080p under-display FaceTime inner camera (f/1.8) | 18MP Center Stage camera (f/1.9) | 18MP Center Stage camera (f/1.9) | 
| Rear Cameras | 48MP main (f/1.6), 48MP ultrawide (f/2.2) | 48MP main with variable aperture (f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, f/4), 48MP ultrawide (f/2.2), 48MP telephoto w/4x optical zoom (f/2.8) | 48MP main with variable aperture (f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, f/4), 48MP ultrawide (f/2.2), 48MP telephoto w/4x optical zoom (f/2.8) | 
| Battery Life Video Playback | Up to 44 hours when using the outer display, up to 31 hours when using the inner display | Up to 36 hours | Up to 45 hours | 
| Size | 6.48 x 4.64 x 0.21 inches open (164.6 x 117.8 x 5.2mm), 3.31 x 4.64 x 0.44 inches closed (84.1 x 117.8 x 11.3mm) | 5.91 x 2.83 x 0.34 inches (150.0 x 71.9 x 8.75 mm) | 6.43 x 3.07 x 0.34 inches (163.4 x 78.0 x 8.75 mm) | 
| Weight | 8.96 ounces (254 grams) | 7.44 ounces (211 grams) | 8.78 ounces (249 grams) | 
| IP Rating | IP68 | IP68 | IP68 | 
| Colors | Night Sky, Star White | Black, Silver, Glacier, Burgundy | Black, Silver, Glacier, Burgundy | 
Price does matter
| Row 0 - Cell 0 | 256GB | 2TB | Dollar Increase | Percentage Increase | 
| iPhone 18 Pro | $1,199 | $2,399 | $1,200 | 100.08% | 
| iPhone 18 Pro Max | $1,299 | $2,499 | $1,200 | 92.38% | 
| iPhone Duo | $1,999 | $3,199 | $1,200 | 60.03% | 
Apple’s latest price adjustments certainly sting, with both traditional flagships seeing a $100 price hike across the board. That means the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max will cost you more than in previous years, as starting prices climb to $1,199 for a 256GB iPhone 18 Pro and $1,299 for the equivalent iPhone 18 Pro Max. At the extreme end, you’re looking at paying $2,399 and $2,499 for the 2TB options on the Pro and Pro Max, respectively.
But despite their higher costs, placing those figures next to the iPhone Duo makes them look like outright bargains that will save you far more cash upfront. While I do applaud Apple for keeping the Duo’s base price competitive at $1,999 for 256GB, that’s still a massive $700 to $800 leap over the Pro models — and it quickly balloons to $3,199 for the 2TB version.
Interestingly, when I ran the numbers, Apple charges a flat $1,200 premium across the board to jump from 256GB to 2TB. On the iPhone 18 Pro, that upgrade literally doubles the phone's price — a massive 100% surge from $1,199 to $2,399. Meanwhile, it represents a 92% hike on the Pro Max and a 60% increase on the Duo.
Unless you genuinely need maximum local capacity, jumping all the way to 2TB is best justified on the Duo.
Tried and true reliability versus utility
 ![iPhone Duo](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/N49opwHV76RM3BfKvL8REa.jpg) 
Obviously, the iPhone Duo introduces a leap in everyday utility that most iPhone users aren’t accustomed to, especially anyone who creates content on the go. Having a folding form factor transforms how I shoot: I can prop it up like a built-in tripod, use the exterior display as a high-res viewfinder for better selfies, and record vlogs while keeping myself framed properly in the shot. That versatility unlocks creative angles I simply can’t get with standard slabs.
Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.
 ![iPhone 18 Pro in Burgundy in hand at Apple Surprise and Shine](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/ZM8ZjrWEbcUw7SrepyDeBM.png) 
Yet, after spending years testing and living with rival foldables, the Duo’s mechanical hinge still gives me pause when it comes to long-term durability. Apple’s engineering looks convincing, but anything with moving parts remains a genuine concern.
In contrast, the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max stick to the familiar playbook. They feature rigid enclosures, proven water resistance, and toughened glass surfaces that have repeatedly demonstrated they can take real-world abuse without cracking under pressure. The Duo certainly wins on novelty and specialized utility, but the Pros offer the kind of rock-solid durability that doesn’t require you to constantly baby your device.
Clever camera utility versus Pro photography
 ![iPhone Duo](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/SoAi2j7o9Dqs6v288A4cEa.jpg) 
I've always been a big fan of the utility and convenience offered by foldable phones, and the iPhone Duo is no exception. It’s incredibly useful to have that external display for better-framed selfies or to show a subject what the final shot will look like, and its 48MP main camera is practically identical to what you’ll find on the Pros. Since that's the workhorse sensor I rely on most, I’m confident it can handle almost any challenging lighting condition. However, the lack of a dedicated telephoto lens on the Duo stings.
Beyond hardware, I can’t overstate how much software elevates the shooting experience. Not only do the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max share the same triple-camera system — complete with a 48MP main sensor featuring a variable aperture — but they also get treated to Apple's full suite of advanced creative tools.
 ![Pro Controls on iPhone 18 Pro](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/HhGRiHZ8d4hXRLpaxyqFEH.png) 
From Pro Controls for manual adjustments and Spatial photo/video capture to LOG video recording and uncompressed ProRAW photos, these are pro-grade features you simply won't get on the Duo.
Same Apple Intelligence, two totally different workflows
 ![iphone duo two apps](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/UDr8c5DLF9rP5aXyr9NwQ5.jpg) 
Under the hood, all three phones run the new A20 Pro chip to handle demanding tasks with ease. Whether you pick up the iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max, or the Duo, you also get the exact same suite of Apple Intelligence and Siri AI features. You won’t miss out on any core capabilities by choosing a traditional slab over the foldable.
Where the software experience dramatically diverges, however, is screen-space utility. The iPhone Duo transforms iOS 27 into an expansive workspace that the Pros simply can’t match. Thanks to dynamic app scaling and true side-by-side multitasking, the Duo lets you effortlessly run two apps at once.
On the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, multitasking is still limited to a single-app flow where you’re forced to minimize one app to interact with another. If your daily routine revolves around juggling multiple workflows simultaneously, the Duo’s software depth provides an undeniable advantage.
Apple indicates which one has the long battery life
 ![iphone 18 pro and pro max side by side](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/sAFnnQsMDkhrRiPhTeYah9.webp) 
Without putting them through proper benchmark testing, it’s hard to say definitively which of the three will offer the greatest battery endurance. Even though Apple doesn’t officially disclose battery capacities, Apple's spec sheet reveals that the iPhone 18 Pro Max will remain the undisputed champion. It’s rated for an astonishing 45 hours of video playback, easily outpacing the smaller iPhone 18 Pro’s respectable 36 hours.
Because it features two displays, the iPhone Duo’s endurance varies depending on which screen you use most. When folded, its outer display offers 44 hours of playback — nearly on par with the Pro Max. But the moment you unfold it to reveal the larger 7.6-inch main screen, battery life takes a noticeable hit, dropping to 31 hours of local playback.
It's a tough call
 ![iPhone 18 pro max](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/9ev3U6oVqLNtW76xrqJLDe.jpg) 
Ultimately, deciding between these three flagships comes down to what you value most: pocketable ergonomics, maximum endurance, or multitasking. The iPhone Duo undeniably adds an exciting layer of utility by turning a compact phone into a canvas for side-by-side apps and hands-free shooting, but that versatility comes with glaring camera compromises. Despite its steep price, the Duo drops the dedicated telephoto lens and misses out on the Pro line's new mechanical variable-aperture system and all the other tools like Pro Controls.
That's why I still recommend the iPhone 18 Pro Max for now as the smartest buy. At just $100 more than the standard iPhone 18 Pro, it easily justifies the modest bump with an expansive display and longer battery life. Then again, it'll likely change once they're put through the Tom's Guide testing.

The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max start at $1,199 and $1,299 respectively, receiving a $100 price hike this year.

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max feature advanced triple-camera systems with a variable aperture and dedicated telephoto lens, which the Duo lacks.

title: Roundup: All The Biggest Reveals From Blizzcon 2026, Including Two Massive Announcements
author: Pure Xbox; Fraser Gilbert
content:
![Roundup: All The Biggest Reveals From Blizzcon 2026, Including Two Massive Announcements](https://images.purexbox.com/8ff1a76cf6f16/roundup-all-the-biggest-reveals-from-blizzcon-2026-including-two-massive-announcements.900x.jpg)
Today marked the start of Blizzcon 2026 over in California, and the Xbox-owned company had a lot of announcements to share as part of the opening ceremony, including two massive announcements regarding Diablo and StarCraft.
Those announcements were that Diablo V is officially in the works with a target release window of 2029, while a new open-world StarCraft game (not an RTS) is aiming for a 2030 release. Xbox has since clarified that StarCraft is definitely coming to console in addition to PC.
Lots of other reveals were sprinkled into the ceremony as well, so we'll list them down below. Not everything here is Xbox-related, but it's still interesting stuff all the same.
New StarCraft Game - 2030 (Console Confirmed)
From the farthest reaches of the stars, a new mission calls. StarCraft returns in 2030 as an original open-world shooter.
Diablo V - 2029
Diablo V is coming in Spring 2029, and it opens somewhere the series has never let us stand: after the loss. Sanctuary has fallen. Diablo has won. The question the game asks is what we become when the world we knew is gone.
New Content Coming To Diablo IV, Plus A Switch 2 Launch
Diablo IV‘s Season of Hell’s Legacy lands September 15 (that’s this Tuesday!) to mark 30 years of Diablo. It brings back the Prime Evils, the Lord of Terror included, along with Deckard Cain, Nightmare Rifts, anniversary rewards, and gear pulled from every era of the series. A little further out, the Amazon joins as the next Diablo IV class in the first half of 2027, javelin in hand.
summary: Blizzcon 2026 kicked off in California with major announcements from the Xbox-owned company, headlined by upcoming entries in the Diablo and StarCraft franchises. Diablo V was officially announced for a Spring 2029 release, while a new open-world StarCraft shooter is slated for 2030 on both PC and consoles. Additionally, Diablo IV is receiving new content, including the Season of Hell's Legacy, the Amazon class in 2027, and a future launch on the Switch 2.
key_points: Diablo V is officially in development with a target release window of Spring 2029.
A new open-world StarCraft shooter is scheduled for 2030 and is confirmed for console release.
Diablo IV's Season of Hell's Legacy launches on September 15 to celebrate 30 years of Diablo.
The Amazon class will be added to Diablo IV in the first half of 2027.
Diablo IV is also getting a Nintendo Switch 2 launch.

title: Deals: iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are on pre-order, iPhone Duo coming soon, here are the alternatives
author: Peter
content:
Pre-orders for the new iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max started this Saturday. And since this is Apple we are talking about, there are no pre-order goodies – the opposite, actually, since Apple raised the iPhone 16, 17 and Air prices by $100. But we won’t be looking at the vanilla models today since the vanilla iPhone 18 isn’t expected until next year.
So, here are the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. They feature Apple’s first 2nm chip, the A20 Pro, which runs at close to 5GHz (it peaks at 4.93GHz) and posted massive Geekbench scores. Additionally, the new models promise longer battery life, especially the Pro Max. And they have a variable aperture for the 48MP 1/1.28” main camera (f/1.5-f/4.0).
By the way, if you want to pick up a carrier deal instead of getting an unlocked iPhone 18 Pro (Max), check out the offers from AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon here.
You can save quite a bit of money by getting a Galaxy S26 instead of an iPhone 18 Pro. Both have 6.3” displays (and both are 120Hz LTPO panels at that), but Samsung’s 10MP 3x/67mm telephoto and 12MP ultra-wide cameras are no match for Apple’s Pro setup, which includes a 48MP 4x/100mm telephoto and a 48MP ultra-wide. Samsung still doesn’t do magnetic charging either.
Looking at the 6.9” offerings, the Galaxy S26 Ultra is also a lot cheaper than the iPhone 18 Pro Max (in fact, it’s cheaper than the small Pro too). The Ultra is a lot more competitive when it comes to cameras – it has a 200MP 1/1.3” main, a 10MP 3x/67mm telephoto plus an additional 50MP 5x/111mm telephoto module and a 50MP ultra-wide. The S26 Ultra also offers unique features like the Privacy Display and the S Pen.
Google also has a 6.3” model, the Pixel 11 Pro. However, it’s pretty light on discounts at the moment. The Tensor G6 mostly fixed the battery efficiency woes of the G5, but performance is still nowhere close to the Apple A20 Pro or the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy. The Pixel does have a more promising set of cameras than the small S26, including a 50MP 1/1.3” main, a 48MP 5x/106mm telephoto and a 48MP ultra-wide. And would you look at that – it has Pixelsnap magnetic wireless charging.
Google’s Pixel 11 Pro XL has a 6.8” screen and the same set of cameras as its smaller sibling.
Given Apple’s prices, you can even consider a foldable instead of an iPhone 18 Pro. The Galaxy Z Flip8 costs the same as the S26 Ultra and while it doesn’t have its cameras (it only has a 50MP 1/1.57” main and a 12MP ultra-wide), it does have a 6.9” inner and a 4.1” cover display. This one is also powered by the Samsung-customized Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 (at least in the US market).
Speaking of foldables, the iPhone Duo is Apple’s first – Cupertino chose to enter this market with a wide foldable. It’s not available yet, though. Pre-orders will start in mid-October and sales will commence a week later. We have some thoughts on the iPhone 18 Pro (Max) vs. iPhone Duo debate that you can peruse while you wait.
Since there aren’t many wide foldable alternatives in the US, the Duo’s main rival is the Galaxy Z Fold8. The Samsung phone is thinner (9.7mm vs. 11.3mm) and much lighter (201g vs. 254g). The 7.6” inner displays on both are nearly identical in size and aspect ratio, but Samsung has had several years to optimize One UI for foldable use. Meanwhile, this is the first time iOS tries to transition apps from a cover to a larger internal display. However, Apple offers stylus support and uses an under-display camera, which are features that Samsung abandoned last year.
The two foldables have comparable cameras with a 48MP main camera with sensor shift OIS for the iPhone Duo and a 50MP camera with lens shift OIS for the Z Fold8. They are joined by a 48MP and a 50MP 120° ultra-wide cameras, respectively. Check out a more detailed comparison between the iPhone Duo and Galaxy Z Fold8 here.
Of course, Samsung also has a larger book-style foldable, the Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra. Despite having a larger 8” inner display (nearly 1:1 aspect ratio) and a larger 6.5” cover display (with a tall and skinny aspect ratio), the Ultra is still a lot lighter than the iPhone Duo (215g vs. 254g). It’s thinner too – in fact, at 8.9mm, the Z Fold8 Ultra is only 0.1mm thicker than the iPhone 18 Pro Max (which weighs 249g, by the way).
This one has a 200MP 1/1.3” main camera plus a dedicated 10MP 3x/67mm telephoto lens, which is missing from both the Z Fold8 and the Duo. There’s a 50MP ultra-wide camera too. The cameras are not as good as the S26 Ultra, but they are better than the Z Fold8 cameras.
Google also makes a large foldable, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. The large 8” inner display is built for multitasking and it enjoys several years of Google working on UI enhancements for foldables. But as we mentioned above, the Tensor G6 is no match for the Apple and Samsung chipsets.
The Pixel 11 Pro Fold doesn’t have the same cameras as the other two 11 Pro models. There’s a 48MP 1/1.56” main, a 10.8MP 5x/112mm telephoto and a 10.5MP 127° ultra-wide. At least it gets to keep the magnetic wireless charging.
Alongside the new phones, Apple also refreshed its wearables lineup. The Apple Watch Series 12 has upgraded optical and electrical heart rate sensors. It also offers several AI-powered audio features – it can detect important sounds for people with hearing issues, it can summarize conversations and it will remember that song you heard half an hour ago.
The Apple Watch Ultra 4 focused on improving battery life. Apple is mum on mAh numbers, but the new model should last up to 50 hours of normal usage (that’s 8 hours longer than the Ultra 3). If you put it in Low Power Mode, it should last up to 84 hours (+12 hours compared to the old model).
Despite Apple having a reputation for making expensive products, the new AirPods 5 are cheaper, while also improving things like noise cancellation, transparency mode, spatial audio and Adaptive EQ. Note that there are two versions – one with USB-C charging and a $20 upgrade that adds wireless charging to the case.
We may get a commission from qualifying sales.
summary: Pre-orders have begun for the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, which feature Apple's new 2nm A20 Pro chip, improved battery life, and a variable aperture main camera. Meanwhile, Apple has also announced the upcoming wide foldable iPhone Duo, refreshed its wearables with the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, and released the more affordable AirPods 5. The article notes various smartphone alternatives from competitors like Samsung and Google, comparing their displays, cameras, and chips against Apple's latest lineup.
key_points: Pre-orders for the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are live, powered by the A20 Pro chip and featuring a variable aperture 48MP main camera.
Apple's first wide foldable, the iPhone Duo, is coming soon with pre-orders starting in mid-October.
Competitor alternatives like the Samsung Galaxy S26 series, Galaxy Z Fold8 models, and Google Pixel 11 Pro series offer different price points, camera setups, and display features.
Apple refreshed its wearables lineup with upgraded heart rate sensors on the Apple Watch Series 12 and extended battery life on the Apple Watch Ultra 4.
The new AirPods 5 are cheaper than previous models while offering improved noise cancellation, spatial audio, and adaptive EQ.

title: ‘World of Warcraft Forever,’ Expanded Version of 2004 Game, Coming in November
author: Jennifer Maas
content:
Blizzard Entertainment will launch “World of Warcraft Forever,” a game set during the first year of the original 2004 “World of Warcraft,” Nov. 4.
The “Forever” project was revealed as the final announcement during the opening ceremony of BlizzCon 2026 at the Anaheim Convention Center on Saturday, but rumors about the title (colloquially known as “World of Warcraft Classic+” among fans speculating online) have been swirling for weeks.
Blizzard’s “Warcraft” chief Holly Longdale said that developers intend for the world of the game to be a main character in “Forever” and noted that in this new MMO it’s “the journey that counts, not the destination.”
Popular on Variety
At launch, include three new zones, over 1,000 new quests, nine new dungeons, two new raids, and a new Skyborne race. The game will have a skill level cap of 60.
Additionally, the “Warcraft” team announced a new campaign for “Warcraft 3,” the first in more than two decades, which launches today.
BlizzCon’s opening ceremony also included announcements about a new “StarCraft” game coming in 2030, “Diablo V” releasing in 2029, and a “Diablo” animated TV series in the works at Netflix.
Variety will be on the ground at BlizzCon Sept. 12-13 and readers can follow along here for our coverage of the event, a celebration of all things Blizzard Entertainment, from “StarCraft” to “Diablo” to “World of Warcraft” to “Overwatch.”
Watch the “World of Warcraft: Forever” trailer via the video below.
summary: Blizzard Entertainment announced "World of Warcraft Forever," an expanded version of the 2004 game set during its first year, launching on November 4. Revealed at BlizzCon 2026, the new MMO will feature a level 60 cap along with new zones, quests, dungeons, raids, and a Skyborne race. Additionally, the company announced a new "Warcraft 3" campaign, future "StarCraft" and "Diablo" projects, and a "Diablo" animated series.
key_points: "World of Warcraft Forever" launches on November 4 and is set during the original 2004 game's first year.
At launch, the game will include three new zones, over 1,000 new quests, nine new dungeons, two new raids, a new Skyborne race, and a level cap of 60.
A new campaign for "Warcraft 3" was also announced and launches today.
Other announcements included a new "StarCraft" game for 2030, "Diablo V" for 2029, and a "Diablo" animated TV series at Netflix.

title: LG responds to TV spying allegations
author: Terrence O'Brien
content:
Earlier this week, Gamers Nexus, Level1Techs, and independent security researchers detailed some alarming findings about how LG’s TVs are logging and uploading data on its users. Now the company is pushing back against those allegations, saying that “Some recent media coverage may have contributed to misconceptions about how LG smart TVs work.”
LG responds to TV spying allegations
The company claims reports about its capturing and uploading audio are misleading.
![LG B4 Press Image 3](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2025/01/LG-B4-Press-Image-3.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400)
![LG B4 Press Image 3](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2025/01/LG-B4-Press-Image-3.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400)
LG released a statement in which it claims that its “TVs do not continuously record or transmit users’ conversations,” and that wake-word detection is all processed locally. However, the word “continuously” is doing a lot of heavy lifting here as Gamers Nexus demonstrated an LG TV keeping extensive logs of ambient conversations long after one would assume its AI assistant had stopped listening.
LG also said that its features like “Automatic Content Recognition (ACR), voice recognition, and interest-based advertising are optional,” and “not enabled by default.” The company says that:
ACR uses audio fingerprinting technology using the TV’s internal audio processor (not a speaker) to identify content and does not collect screenshots, screen recordings, video recordings, voice recordings, or other audio recordings from the TV.
The company did not address broader concerns about how much data it collects, who it shares it with, the potential for bad actors to exploit its features, or the misleading way in which its privacy options are presented.
summary: LG has responded to recent findings by security researchers and tech outlets regarding its smart TVs logging and uploading user data. The company stated that its TVs do not continuously record conversations and that features like voice recognition and Automatic Content Recognition are optional. However, LG did not address broader concerns about overall data collection, data sharing, or how privacy options are presented.
key_points: Security researchers and tech channels detailed alarming data logging practices by LG smart TVs.
LG denied continuously recording or transmitting conversations, stating wake-word detection is processed locally.
The company emphasized that features like ACR, voice recognition, and interest-based advertising are optional and not enabled by default.
LG failed to address broader concerns regarding data collection amounts, third-party sharing, and privacy option presentation.

title: Samsung Trolls Apple by Hiring 'Tim Cook' to Endorse Galaxy Z Fold 8
author: Michael Kan
content:
Samsung is responding to the iPhone Duo by circulating a cheeky ad that features a “Tim Cook” endorsing the Galaxy Fold Z 8—except it’s not former Apple CEO Tim Cook.
Instead, the Samsung ad stars Tim Cook from Palmerston North, New Zealand. “Hi, I’m Tim Cook. From Palmy,” the man says, while wearing glasses and clothing similar to the well-known Apple exec. In the ad, the New Zealander reviews the Galaxy Z Fold 8, lampooning Apple's usual hyperbolic language.
“This thing is the best of both worlds,” the New Zealander says. “Best phone I’ve ever had. You can quote me. Tim Cook from Palmerston North.”
Samsung published the ad on social media a day after Apple finally debuted its long-rumored foldable, the iPhone Duo, which is already creating buzz. Analysts expect the Duo to boost the adoption of foldable phones, which currently account for 2% of the total smartphone market, according to Counterpoint Research.
Samsung began selling its first foldable phone in 2019, giving it ample time to tweak and improve the product. But Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, says the iPhone Duo is the “most transformational change to iPhone since the original." Hence, the companies face a looming battle for buyers, though their $2,000 price tags may limit their appeal.
summary: Samsung released a new ad featuring a New Zealander named Tim Cook to endorse the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and mock Apple's marketing language. The ad was published shortly after Apple debuted its long-rumored foldable phone, the iPhone Duo. Both companies are now competing for buyers in the foldable smartphone market, despite potential limitations from their $2,000 price tags.
key_points: Samsung's ad stars a New Zealand resident named Tim Cook who humorously endorses the Galaxy Z Fold 8.
The advertisement was released a day after Apple debuted its new foldable phone, the iPhone Duo.
Foldable phones currently account for 2% of the total smartphone market.
Both the Samsung and Apple foldable devices feature $2,000 price tags.

title: iPhone Duo vs Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: How the flagflip foldables compare
author: Alex Lee
content:
Samsung has had an eight-year head start on Apple in making foldable phones. But after years of rumours, Apple has finally entered the ring, and it’s taking aim at the South Korean tech giant.
Announced on 9 September, the iPhone Duo is Apple’s first foldable iPhone, and in form factor alone, it’s a direct rival to the recently launched Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8. Boasting a book-style design, it transforms from a regular smartphone into a near-iPad mini-sized device when you unfold it.
But while they might work – conceptually, anyway – in much the same way, Apple and Samsung have presented two very different smartphones in terms of execution. Based on what Apple has announced, I’ve compared the iPhone Duo and Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8’s displays, cameras, software, performance, battery life and price.
Read more: iPhone 18 Pro vs iPhone 17 Pro
![iPhone Duo](<https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/11/16/40/iphone-duo.png?quality=75&width=296&auto=webp 296w>)
Apple’s first-ever foldable iPhone features a 5.4in outer display with a large 7.6in inner screen. It’s expensive and considerably heavier than Samsung’s alternative, but has a flexible hinge, Apple Pencil support and some clever software designed specifically for the folding form factor. It starts from £1,999 and goes on sale in October.
Key specifications
- Outer display: 5.4in OLED, 120Hz
- Inner display: 7.6in OLED, 120Hz
- Processor: A20 Pro
- Cameras: 48MP main, 48MP ultrawide
- Storage: 256GB, 512GB, 1TB, 2TB
- Weight: 254g
- Water and dust resistance: IP68
![z fold 8](<https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/07/31/11/27/z-fold-8.png?quality=75&width=296&auto=webp 296w>)
Samsung’s eighth-generation book-style foldable is slimmer, lighter and £300 cheaper than the iPhone Duo. Like the Duo, it features a passport-style design, and its software is brilliantly polished with picture-perfect folding. I don’t like the lack of a telephoto camera, limited dust protection and lack of S Pen support, however – the latter two you get with the iPhone Duo. It starts at £1,699 for the 256GB model.
Key specifications
- Outer display: 5.5in AMOLED, 120Hz
- Inner display: 7.6in AMOLED, 120Hz
- Processor: Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy
- Cameras: 50MP main, 50MP ultrawide
- Storage: 256GB, 512GB, 1TB
- Weight: 201g
- Water and dust resistance: IP48
iPhone Duo vs Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: Design and displays
It’s a little tricky to know who actually came first when it comes to the passport-sized form factor. While Samsung launched the Galaxy Z Fold 8 a few months before Apple announced the iPhone Duo, it’s been known since early 2025 that Apple was working on a passport-sized book-style foldable.
In any case, they have very similar dimensions. Folded, the iPhone Duo has a 5.4in outer display, with the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 featuring a slightly larger 5.5in cover screen. Open them up, though, and both give you a huge 7.6in OLED display, essentially transforming the phones into mini tablets.
But they don’t actually look all that similar. The iPhone Duo has a somewhat controversial asymmetric silhouette. The left side is straight, while the right side is curved, making it look like a “D”. The Samsung Z Fold 8 is all right angles, all the way round.
![The iPhone Duo is Apple's first foldable phone](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/10/16/53/Screenshot-2026-09-10-at-17-43-19.png)
Both phones have adaptive refresh rates of up to 120Hz and can reach up to 3,000 nits of peak brightness.
The most interesting thing is that the iPhone Duo’s inner screen features a nano-texture finish, reducing glare and helping to minimise the visibility of the crease. “From a distance, the display on the inside looks a little darker than a normal iPhone screen. It isn’t, it’s a matte finish that keeps reflections down,” Andrew Griffin said in his first impressions.
While I’ve not tried the iPhone Duo yet, that matte finish does make it look dimmer and duller, though that will have to be tested at a later date. Samsung’s inner display, on the other hand, is glossy like the cover screen. Samsung has put an anti-reflective treatment over the top, with new Flex Titanium technology reinforcing the folding display and helping to reduce the visibility of the crease. Griffin says there’s no visible crease on the Duo at all. While the Z Fold 8 crease is very nearly invisible, you can still see it if you go looking.
Apple has also hidden the selfie camera underneath the Duo’s inner display – and it seems from early coverage that Apple would like users to avoid using that one entirely, using the rear cameras to take selfies instead (more on that below). Samsung, on the other hand, has a conventional 10MP camera embedded in its folding display.
There are differences in the hinges too. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 almost forces you to click it into place when you open it fully to 180 degrees, meaning you can’t prop it open at different angles in the traditional Flex Mode anymore. I found flipping it over and standing it on its edges like a teepee was a way around this.
![The Z Fold 8 has more squared-off edges](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/07/31/14/51/Samsung-Galaxy-Z-Fold-8-review.png)
Apple, however, has designed the Duo to work in loads of partially folded positions, so you can fold it into a seated position like a laptop, prop it up on its edges like a tent or fold it like a book.
One of my biggest gripes with the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is that both speakers sit on the same half of the phone. Open it up into landscape and they both fire from the left side of the display, so there isn’t much stereo separation when watching videos.
Apple fixes this by placing the iPhone Duo’s two speakers diagonally on opposite halves of the phone. When it’s unfolded, the speakers sit at opposite corners of the display, which should provide much better stereo separation when watching films and TV shows. I’ll need to listen to them myself to see how good they actually sound.
The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 does have one pretty huge advantage, however, and that’s the weight. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 weighs just 201g, while the iPhone Duo weighs a hefty 254g. That’s a 53g difference, and given I already found the Fold 8 impressively light for a folding phone, I suspect you’ll notice it.
The iPhone Duo is a lot thicker when shut as well – that’s the first thing that caught my eye when I saw pictures of the device. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 measures 9.7mm when folded and 4.5mm when unfolded. The iPhone Duo is more than 1.5mm thicker when shut (11.3mm folded and 5.2mm unfolded).
That said, the iPhone Duo has much better protection against dust and sand. It has an IP68 rating, while the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is only rated IP48, so you won’t want to take Samsung’s foldable anywhere near the beach.
And, in a slightly bizarre role reversal, Apple is the one offering stylus support. Apple has announced that the iPhone Duo will work with the USB-C Apple Pencil later this year – Samsung dropped S Pen support from the Galaxy Z Fold 8 completely.
The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 comes in four colours – lavender, graphite, cream and pistachio – with the latter reserved as a Samsung Store exclusive.
The iPhone Duo only comes in two colours – star white and night sky (black).
Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 is a slimmer, lighter foldable, but the iPhone Duo appears to provide a better overall design experience, with a more flexible hinge, better speaker placement, matte inner display and Apple Pencil support, as well as an IP68 rating.
iPhone Duo vs Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: Cameras
Both the iPhone Duo and Z Fold 8 feature two rear cameras instead of the triple-camera systems on their respective flagship models.
The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 features a 50MP f/1.8 main camera and a 50MP f/1.9 ultrawide. The iPhone Duo is kitted out with a 48MP f/1.6 main camera and a 48MP f/2.2 ultrawide camera. Both feature a 2x optical-quality zoom – no telephoto.
That missing telephoto lens was one of my biggest complaints when I reviewed the Galaxy Z Fold 8. The 2x zoom is perfectly serviceable, but you notice less detail at 5x and 10x digital zoom.
![You can barely see the crease on the Z Fold 8](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/07/31/15/08/z-fold-8-opened.png)
The iPhone Duo may have the same issue. You can shoot at 0.5x, 1x and 2x, and there’s a 10x digital zoom, but there’s no equivalent of the 8x optical-quality zoom on the iPhone 18 Pro. The iPhone Duo’s main camera does at least have a wider f/1.6 aperture, as well as sensor-shift optical image stabilisation, so it might take better-quality low-light photos, but I’ll have to test that.
On the Galaxy Z Fold 8, you can use the cover screen as a viewfinder while taking selfies with the rear cameras. Apple has taken the same idea and pushed it further. The iPhone Duo’s Preview feature puts a live view of the shot on the outer display so the person you’re photographing can frame themselves in the shot, but you can also flip the phone and use the rear cameras for higher-quality selfies, something Apple has been encouraging content creators to do in its demos.
Apple’s also rolled out a Smart Take feature that uses on-device AI to work out when everyone is ready and automatically takes the photo, meaning you don’t have to sprint back into frame after setting a timer. Kid Cue also plays animations on the outer display to persuade children to actually look at the camera.
Samsung has some fun camera tricks too. My FanCam can take a wide landscape video and track one specific person in the frame after the footage is taken, reframing it into a vertical clip for socials.
The iPhone Duo can record 4K Dolby Vision at up to 120fps on its main camera. It also supports Cinematic mode at up to 4K 60fps and can shoot 4K Dolby Vision time-lapses. Samsung can shoot up to 8K video, but it doesn’t have the same Dolby Vision support.
You won’t get a fully-fledged flagship camera experience from either phone. The iPhone Duo might tip the balance on specs alone, however. It has a wider main aperture, better video features and uses the outer display better. Whether it actually takes better pictures, we’ll have to wait to find out.
iPhone Duo vs Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: Performance and software
Both phones are powered by the latest flagship chips from Apple and Qualcomm. The iPhone Duo has the same A20 Pro chip found inside the iPhone 18 Pro. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is powered by the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy.
![The iPhone Duo only comes in two colours](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/11/16/39/iphone-duo.png)
Apple says the A20 Pro’s six-core CPU is up to 20 per cent faster than the A19 Pro and its seven-core GPU is up to 40 per cent faster and more power efficient. There’s also a new dual 16-core Neural Engine for running Apple Intelligence features on-device. The iPhone Duo also has a vapour chamber to keep everything cool, with Apple claiming up to 35 per cent better sustained performance than the iPhone 17 Pro.
I’ve already put the Galaxy Z Fold 8 through its paces, and the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy is seriously quick. Apps open instantly and multitasking is smooth. I haven’t tested the iPhone Duo yet, but given it has the same A20 Pro chip as Apple’s flagship iPhone 18 Pro, I doubt performance is going to be a problem.
Software is much more interesting than the performance specs. Samsung’s had years to perfect how the folding experience works on the Z Fold 8, and it’s brilliant. You can run apps side by side using Multi Window, drag and drop content between them and move seamlessly between the cover and inner displays.
One UI 9’s Multi Window is ultra versatile, and the tech giant’s Galaxy AI Now Nudge feature can recognise what you’re doing and suggest actions in another window, so you don’t need to constantly move between apps.
Apple might be late to the party, but it always does its homework. iOS 27 has been redesigned specifically for the iPhone Duo. The dock and app controls are now on the right side of the phone, making better use of the display (although I’m not sure if this will make it more difficult for lefties to use the phone).
And you can finally multitask on an iPhone. The new Split View lets you run two apps side by side and even save pairs of apps you regularly use together as a single app.
![You can prop both up like a tent](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/07/31/15/29/z-fold-8-teepee.png)
Apple also demonstrated how Zoom can now show both a presentation and the people on a call; Slack can fit more of your workspace onto the screen; and Netflix can expand across the entire display. Apps also adjust to the position of the hinge, which is fascinating to see, especially in the seated fold position.
One neat thing I’ve spotted from the demonstrations is how much more visually cohesive the experience looks on the iPhone Duo. “That software experience even extends to the process of opening and closing the phone. Apple has done an astonishing job in ensuring that the phone knows it is opening, and mirrors the content on the little screen onto the big one, so that you almost forget they’re not actually the same thing,” Griffin said in his hands-on review. The inner screen on the Z Fold 8, for example, remains black when you start opening it up, only activating when it’s halfway open.
They may be similar in terms of raw specs and performance, but when it comes to software, Apple may take the lead – again, I’ll have to try it for myself.
iPhone Duo vs Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: Battery life
Apple doesn’t typically reveal the actual capacity of its batteries, but the iPhone Duo does feature one battery on either side of the device, both working together as one.
The company says you’ll get up to 24 hours of typical use, or up to 31 hours of video playback using the inner display and a whopping 44 hours using the outer display.
Samsung is a little more forthcoming with the numbers. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 has a 4,800mAh silicon-carbon battery, which Samsung says delivers up to 26 hours of video playback.
It’s difficult to compare Apple and Samsung’s video playback figures directly because they use different testing methodologies, but Apple’s battery claims are huge if true.
![](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/11/16/21/iphone-duo-white.png)
The Galaxy Z Fold 8 supports 45W wired charging. It can reach up to 63 per cent in 30 minutes. It also supports 20W wireless charging.
Apple says the iPhone Duo can get to 50 per cent in roughly 20 minutes using a 60W-capable or higher adapter. It also supports MagSafe and Qi2 wireless charging, potentially getting to 50 per cent in 30 minutes. Unlike the Galaxy Z Fold 8, the magnets are built directly into the phone, so you don’t need a magnetic case to take advantage of Qi2 charging, though you can charge wirelessly at up to 20W.
iPhone Duo vs Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: Price
Neither phone is cheap, but you may gulp when you hear the iPhone Duo’s price.
The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is £1,699 for 256GB of storage, £1,869 for 512GB and £2,209 for 1TB. That’s already pretty expensive, but the iPhone Duo makes it sound frankly cheap.
The iPhone Duo starts at £1,999 for the 256GB model, but the 512GB model is an eye-watering £2,199, with the 1TB model costing an enormous £2,599. There’s even a 2TB model for £3,199, which is more expensive than some of the most expensive MacBook Pro laptops and almost as expensive as the Apple Vision Pro.
![The Z Fold 8 is more than 1.5mm thinner than the iPhone Duo](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/07/31/15/28/Z-Fold-8.png)
That means there’s a £300 difference between the entry-level iPhone Duo and Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8. The 512GB iPhone Duo costs £330 more than the equivalent Fold 8 and the 1TB model costs £390 more.
Samsung is the obvious winner on price, but £1,699 is still an absurd amount of money for a foldable phone with just two cameras. We’ll see if Apple can justify that £300 premium after testing.
iPhone Duo vs Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: Which should you buy?
The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is thinner, significantly lighter and £300 cheaper, and Samsung also has years of experience making foldables, which shows in the Z Fold 8’s polish.
But the iPhone Duo looks really compelling. It has a more versatile hinge, better dust protection, a better speaker array and Apple Pencil support. Apple appears to have put a lot of thought into how iOS works over the two displays as well.
For Android users, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the only passport foldable you’ll want to buy, and iPhone users finally have a foldable of their own. If you’re not wedded to either operating system, the iPhone Duo looks a little more exciting. I’ll reserve judgement until I get a chance to review the iPone Duo.
summary: Apple has entered the foldable market with the launch of the iPhone Duo, directly competing with the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8. While both devices feature a book-style passport format with dual 120Hz displays, they differ significantly in dimensions, hinge design, durability ratings, and software features. The iPhone Duo introduces a matte inner screen finish, an IP68 dust-and-water resistance rating, and Apple Pencil support, whereas the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is notably lighter, slimmer, and cheaper.
key_points: The iPhone Duo starts at £1,999, features an A20 Pro chip, and boasts an IP68 dust and water resistance rating along with Apple Pencil support.
The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 starts at £1,699, is powered by a Snapdragon chip, and is significantly lighter and thinner than Apple's device.
Both smartphones feature a passport-style book design with 5.4 to 5.5-inch outer screens and large 7.6-inch inner OLED displays supporting 120Hz refresh rates.

The iPhone Duo includes a matte inner finish to reduce glare and a more versatile multi-angle hinge, while Samsung's Z Fold 8 offers refined multitasking software and an anti-reflective glossy display.

title: After PlayStation tells fans they don't own digital games, one Consumer Rights group is tracking all the times Sony said the opposite
author: Kaan Serin
content:
Last month, Sony argued that "reasonable consumers" already know they don't really own the digital goods they paid for. The Consumer Rights wiki has now made a list collecting more than 30 examples where Sony told customers they do, in fact, own the digital games they paid for.
A class action lawsuit recently filed against Sony alleged the PlayStation Store isn't clear enough about the fact that digital purchases don't equal digital ownership. Once a player makes a purchase on the PlayStation Store, they're paying for a digital license that's revocable at any point in time - the purchase doesn't guarantee you'll have access to a particular game or DLC or cosmetic pack forever.
Sony's legal team fired back, arguing that it's not breaking any laws around digital ownership because "reasonable consumers would not be misled" by the storefront's small print disclosures. (You know, the links to the company's Terms of Service and Software Product Licensing Agreement that show up just before you pay for something on the PlayStation Store.)
Seemingly in response to those arguments, the Consumer Rights wiki has now created a "non-exhaustive table of references on Sony's site to 'owning' digital games." The list includes more than 30 occasions in which Sony's site has said something along the lines of, "View a broadcast for a game you own through the game's hub," or, "If you own the PS4 and PS5 versions of the same game, here's how to switch between them…"
One of the more recent examples can be found in Marvel's Wolverine's FAQ section: "Standard Edition owners can also upgrade to the Digital Deluxe Edition content."
The lawsuit claimants said Sony was in breach of a California Law that made it "unlawful for a seller of a digital good to advertise or offer for sale a digital good to a purchaser with the terms 'buy,' 'purchase,' or any other term which a reasonable person would understand to confer an unrestricted ownership interest in the digital good." (Reasonability doesn't seem like something you could measure in court, but I digress.) A digital vendor can get around the law by giving customers clear information about the licenses they're paying for. We'll see how the suit plays out over the coming weeks and months.
summary: Following a class action lawsuit alleging the PlayStation Store misleads buyers about digital game ownership, Sony argued that reasonable consumers know digital purchases are revocable licenses. In response, the Consumer Rights wiki compiled a list of over 30 instances where Sony previously told customers they own their digital games. The lawsuit centers on whether terms like 'buy' or 'purchase' deceptively imply unrestricted ownership under California law.
key_points: A class action lawsuit alleges the PlayStation Store fails to clearly communicate that digital purchases are revocable licenses rather than permanent ownership.
Sony's legal team argued that reasonable consumers would not be misled by storefront disclosures and terms of service.
The Consumer Rights wiki created a list of more than 30 examples where Sony's website explicitly used terms indicating customers 'own' their digital games.
The lawsuit claims Sony violated a California law regarding the use of misleading sales terms like 'buy' or 'purchase' for digital goods.

title: Sony reportedly ditched Hideo Kojima's Physint following missed deadlines, bloated budgets, and Death Stranding 1&2 missing sales expectations
author: Connor Makar
content:
Following Sony's announcement earlier this week that it had "stepped away" from Kojima Production's previously PlayStation-exclusive "action espionage" Physint, a new report has claimed Sony's decision was the result of concerns over "budget, potential profitability and exclusivity."
Speaking to Bloomberg, sources familiar with the project said a major factor behind the decision was the commercial performance of Hidea Kojima's prior two games, Death Stranding and Death Stranding 2. While both were critically acclaimed, they reportedly did not pull in the revenue Sony expected.
![Cover image for YouTube video](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/FGa58WkfmYU/hqdefault.jpg) Physint - Kojima Productions Announcement | State of Play 2024
It's also claimed Physint was over budget, and had missed deadlines despite "being years away from release." The game was also set to be published on other platforms aside from the PlayStation, and Sony was "reluctant" to invest hundreds of millions of dollars into a project that wouldn't be exclusive to its console ecosystem.
This follows reports earlier this year that Sony has abandoned its previous multi-format approach, and would no longer release its single-player PlayStation games on PC, instead keeping them PS5-exclusive. Physint, as an IP owned by Kojima Productions, would have run against this strategy. Bloomberg also notes that while Hideo Kojima and Sony have had a tight business relationship for decades, the PlayStation executives close to Kojima have left in recent years.
Sony has also faced significant software-related troubles in recent years, including 2024's Concord flop and Marathon's continued struggles, which has led the company to implement stricter production milestones, according to Bloomberg. This, in turn, has resulted in several game cancellations.
Additionally, Bloomberg notes the hardware cost crisis caused by the generative AI industry has made consoles more expensive, both for consumers to buy and for Sony to produce. As a result, the company is now focused on maximising revenue from its existing userbase, rather than pushing to grow its audience.
Enter Xbox, which swooped in to pick up Physint following Sony's departure from the project. Microsoft's gaming arm has struggled with its own share of controversies in recent times, including sweeping layoffs and the ongoing impact of BTS boycotts.
According to Bloomberg, Physint was seen as a good investment by Xbox due to its presence on PC, and its film and television rights, which aligns with prior statements from Xbox CEO Asha Sharma on pushing the company's franchises into different mediums.
An Xbox spokesperson even provided Bloomberg a statement when asked, saying, "Betting on Kojima-san is an easy call. We believe in his team’s ability to build AAA games with groundbreaking, new IP and we believe in OD, Physint, and our growing partnership."
summary: Sony reportedly walked away from Hideo Kojima's upcoming action espionage game Physint due to concerns over bloated budgets, missed deadlines, and the underwhelming sales performance of Death Stranding 1 and 2. Additionally, Sony was reluctant to fund a non-exclusive project amid a broader shift back toward PlayStation-exclusive software. Following Sony's departure, Xbox stepped in to pick up the project, citing the game's multi-platform presence and its associated film and television rights.
key_points: Sony stepped away from Physint due to missed deadlines, over-budget issues, and profit concerns.
Death Stranding and Death Stranding 2 reportedly failed to meet Sony's revenue expectations.
Sony shifted away from multi-format releases, making Physint's non-exclusive status a conflict.
Xbox picked up the Physint project following Sony's departure.
Xbox values Physint for its PC presence and potential across film and television mediums.

title: Apple on wide Android foldables beating iPhone Duo; 'they got the aspect ratio'
author: Will Sattelberg
content:
![](https://9to5google.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2026/09/iphone-duo-galaxy-z-fold-8-1.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=1600) 
If it feels like it’s been a quiet week for Android news, it’s not just because Monday was a holiday in the US. As is often the case, pretty much everyone got out of the way of Apple’s latest iPhone announcement, which saw the company launch its first-ever foldable. Joining the party this late is down to lead to some questions towards the company’s leadership, but a new interview with Apple’s fresh-faced CEO helps shine some light on how the brand views its Duo competitors.
The folks at Tom’s Guide and TechRadar sat down with Apple CEO John Ternus and SVP of Marketing Greg Joswiak to dish on the iPhone Duo, and the pair had some thoughts for their Android-based competition. Ternus started with a comment on what he sees as “cheap-feeling plastic” surfaces on devices like the Pixel 11 Pro Fold or Galaxy Z Fold 8, praising the Duo’s nanotexture finish as the solution to the typical polymer displays foldables are required to use. Ternus also pointed out that the device was largely kept secret, though that “they” — Samsung and other rivals, presumably — managed to learn about the aspect ratio ahead of time.
Ternus and Joz also commented on the software side of the device, pointing to their relationships with developers as a reason the iPhone Duo will outperform its competitors when the device launches next month. The pair specifically highlighted Slack, Netflix, and Zoom as apps that will be optimized for the foldable come day one, though early adopters should definitely prep themselves for some familiar black borders. Apparently, the month and a half gap between the Duo’s announcement and its launch date is also part of the plan, echoing back to the three-month gap the iPad received in 2010 to give third-parties time to make changes to their apps.
Apple also sees the redesigned iOS experience on the Duo as the smartest way to approach foldable software, calling it “incredibly intuitive” and helping to make the overall experience “continuous. I will say, paired with some truly slick animations when opening the display, Apple’s foldable iPhone could have a leg up on its Android competition in that regard, and I’m fascinated to see how companies like Samsung and Google respond to a company as traditionally conservative in its design doing something as massive as moving the dock. Those answers, I would think, will likely arrive throughout 2027.
The entire interview, embedded above, is worth a watch, even if I assume most of the people reading this article likely aren’t interested in switching to the iPhone Duo. Ternus and Joz also tackle the stylus question — in their eyes, Jobs’ famous quote about using a stylus with a smartphone doesn’t apply here — and claim they see the Duo as “a great value.” Plus, it’s a chance to get better acquainted with Apple’s new CEO outside of following orders in renaming Lake Ontario in Apple Maps, just as the Sundar Pichai-led Google did last month.
More on iPhone Duo:
![Add 9to5Google as a preferred source on Google](https://9to5google.com/wp-content/themes/ninetofive/dist/images/google-preferred-source-badge-dark.png) 
![Add 9to5Google as a preferred source on Google](https://9to5google.com/wp-content/themes/ninetofive/dist/images/google-preferred-source-badge-light.png)
summary: Apple executives John Ternus and Greg Joswiak discussed the newly announced iPhone Duo in an interview with Tom’s Guide and TechRadar. They praised the device's nanotexture finish and emphasized their strong developer relationships to ensure day-one app optimization. The leaders also defended the redesign of iOS for foldables and noted that the launch gap provides time for third-party developers to adapt.
key_points: Apple CEO John Ternus and SVP of Marketing Greg Joswiak highlighted the iPhone Duo's nanotexture finish as superior to the polymer displays on rival Android foldables.
Apple pointed to strong developer relationships with apps like Slack, Netflix, and Zoom to ensure day-one optimization for the Duo.
The month and a half gap between the Duo's announcement and launch is intentionally designed to give third-party developers time to update their apps.
Apple executives defended the redesigned, intuitive iOS experience on the foldable as a continuous and smart software approach.

title: Finally, a BMW Z4 M? Bovensiepen has revealed the new Spider | Autocar
author: Felix Page
content:
Bovensiepen, the new marque set up by the founders of Alpina, has turned the BMW Z4 into a 429bhp collector special called the Spider.
The brand's third car – after the £320k Zagato coupé and £144k 05 GT estate – is its first convertible, but it can trace its roots back 20 years to the Z4-based Alpina Roadster S that its creators produced in their previous guise.
Just 99 examples will be produced, with deliveries beginning in early 2027, but the Spider is priced well below its range-mates, at the equivalent of £99,000 in Germany – roughly the same as a new BMW M4 convertible.
The firm says that cars are constantly becoming "bigger, heavier and increasingly influenced by SUV designs" and as a result "a vehicle class that for decades epitomised the most immediate form of driving is disappearing: the lightweight, two-seater roadster".
Pledging to preserve this endangered species, Bovensiepen has overhauled the most recent Z4 – which bowed out of production earlier this year – "entirely in the spirit of 'fine driving'".
![](https://www.autocar.co.uk/sites/autocar.co.uk/files/styles/body-image/public/bovensiepen_spider_03.jpg?itok=7s4RpT9b)
It is based on the top-spec Z4 M40i, with output from its 3.0-litre straight six ramped up substantially to 429bhp and 428lb ft.
That's enough to give a 0-62mph time of 4.2sec and a maximum speed of 183mph, making it quicker than any previous iteration of the Z4.
Modifications to the intake system, meanwhile, mean the engine can "breathe freely" and the re-engineered exhaust system has been optimised for flow while "at the same time delivering an exhilarating, sporty sound".
Cooling has been improved, too, to ensure the Spider can always offer peak performance, while an optional Performance Pack brings enhanced heat management for the differential, to boost its performance in high-load situations.
The Spider rides on retuned dampers for improved responsiveness, supported by sticky Michelin Pilot Sport 4S tyres wrapped around the lightweight forged wheels. The brakes can be optionally upgraded to high-performance items too.
The Z4 was latterly available with a six-speed manual gearbox, but the Spider comes with the standard ZF eight-speed auto.
In characteristic Alpina/Bovensiepen fashion, the Z4's interior has been retained but retrimmed in a selection of upmarket materials, including Vernasca leather for the seats, Lavalina for the steering wheel and Alcantara for the windscreen surround.
summary: Bovensiepen, established by the founders of Alpina, has introduced the Spider, a 429bhp collector special based on the BMW Z4. Limited to 99 units with deliveries starting in early 2027, the car is priced at roughly £99,000 in Germany. The vehicle features performance upgrades including a tuned 3.0-litre straight-six engine, retuned dampers, and an upmarket retrimmed interior.
key_points: The Bovensiepen Spider is a limited-run convertible based on the top-spec BMW Z4 M40i, with only 99 examples being produced.
It features an upgraded 3.0-litre straight-six engine delivering 429bhp and 428lb ft of torque, achieving 0-62mph in 4.2 seconds.
Deliveries are scheduled to begin in early 2027 with a price equivalent to £99,000 in Germany.
The car includes mechanical enhancements such as retuned dampers, improved cooling, lightweight forged wheels, and an optional Performance Pack.
The interior retains the Z4 layout but is retrimmed with upmarket materials including Vernasca leather, Lavalina, and Alcantara.
